source_report: English edition of Rice and Maize Disease Features and Sources (originally Korean)
note: One feature row = one feature from one source. Descriptions are English renderings of Korean paraphrases; quotes are 15 words or fewer. 'Unconfirmed' marks unverified items.

diseases.intro: The Korean official descriptions are two NCPMS pages (leaf blast and panicle blast, with identical text); lesion-size figures appear only in an overseas source (Sri Lanka Department of Agriculture).

features.description: Forms lesions on aerial parts such as leaves, panicles, panicle branches, nodes and grains; the most common forms are leaf, panicle and panicle-branch blast
features.source_name: RDA National Crop Pest Management System, paddy rice leaf blast (NCPMS-Leaf blast)

features.description: Attacks all aerial parts including leaves, leaf collar, nodes, neck and parts of the panicle, and sometimes the leaf sheath
features.short_quote: "all above ground parts of a rice plant"
features.source_name: IRRI Rice Knowledge Bank, "Blast (leaf and collar)" (IRRI-Leaf/collar blast)

features.description: Leaf lesions are spindle-shaped. In the chronic type the margin is red; in the acute type fine gray mold (conidia) covers the lesion surface
features.growth_stage: Not stated (paddy field from late June; see timing row)
features.source_name: RDA National Crop Pest Management System, paddy rice leaf blast (NCPMS-Leaf blast)

features.description: Early lesions are white to gray-green spots with dark green borders
features.short_quote: "white to gray-green lesions or spots, with dark green borders"
features.source_name: IRRI Rice Knowledge Bank, "Blast (leaf and collar)" (IRRI-Leaf/collar blast)

features.description: Older lesions are elliptical to spindle-shaped, with white to gray centers and red to brown or necrotic borders. Some are diamond-shaped, wide in the middle and pointed at both ends. As lesions enlarge and merge, the whole leaf dies
features.source_name: IRRI Rice Knowledge Bank, "Blast (leaf and collar)" (IRRI-Leaf/collar blast)

features.description: Leaf spots start as small white, gray or bluish specks. Under humid conditions they enlarge quickly into elliptical or diamond-shaped spots or linear lesions pointed at both ends, with gray to white centers and narrow brown borders. In severe cases leaves and whole plants die
features.short_quote: "white, gray or blue-tinged spots"
features.growth_stage: Seedling to late tillering (leaf blast phase)
features.source_name: LSU AgCenter Pub. 3153 "Blast of Rice" (Groth & Hollier, 6/10) (LSU-Blast)

features.description: Spindle-shaped leaf spots with brown or reddish-brown to yellowish-brown borders, ashy centers and pointed ends. Fully developed lesions are usually 1.0–1.5 cm long and 0.3–0.5 cm wide. Symptoms vary with growth stage, cultivar susceptibility and environment
features.short_quote: "1.0 -1.5 cm in length and 0.3 -0.5cm in breadth"
features.source_name: Sri Lanka Department of Agriculture, Rice Research & Development Institute, Rice blast page (DOA-SriLanka)

features.description: Leaf blast lesions are usually elongated with pointed ends. Brown spot lesions are rounder, brown, and surrounded by a yellow halo
features.source_name: IRRI Rice Knowledge Bank, "Blast (leaf and collar)" (IRRI-Leaf/collar blast)
features.location_in_source: "How to identify" comparison paragraph below the photo

features.description: With severe leaf blast the whole hill turns reddish and stops growing (stunting, "jwaji")
features.source_name: RDA National Crop Pest Management System, paddy rice leaf blast (NCPMS-Leaf blast)

features.description: Leaf blast can kill plants from the seedling to the tillering stage
features.source_name: IRRI Rice Knowledge Bank, "Blast (leaf and collar)" (IRRI-Leaf/collar blast)

features.description: The leaf collar becomes discolored like neck symptoms, and the attached leaf blade also discolors and dies
features.source_name: LSU AgCenter Pub. 3153 "Blast of Rice" (Groth & Hollier, 6/10) (LSU-Blast)

features.description: The IRRI leaf/collar fact sheet only shows a "Collar blast" photo and does not describe collar lesions in text
features.source_name: IRRI Rice Knowledge Bank, "Blast (leaf and collar)" (IRRI-Leaf/collar blast)

features.description: Dark-brown lesions form on nodes, which break easily; under high humidity the surface is covered with gray mold
features.source_name: RDA National Crop Pest Management System, paddy rice panicle blast (NCPMS-Panicle blast; text identical to the leaf blast page)

features.description: Node infection appears as bands, with black to gray-brown lesions. Infected nodes can cause the culm supporting the panicle to break
features.short_quote: "Node infection occurs in banded pattern."
features.source_name: IRRI Rice Knowledge Bank, "Blast (node and neck)" (IRRI-Node/neck blast)

features.description: Infected nodes discolor and shrivel, and plants often lodge
features.source_name: LSU AgCenter Pub. 3153 "Blast of Rice" (Groth & Hollier, 6/10) (LSU-Blast)

features.description: Infected nodes turn black and rot
features.source_name: Sri Lanka Department of Agriculture, Rice Research & Development Institute, Rice blast page (DOA-SriLanka)

features.description: The neck and panicle branches dry out light brown, and under humid conditions gray mold appears on the surface
features.source_name: RDA National Crop Pest Management System, paddy rice panicle blast (NCPMS-Panicle blast; text identical to the leaf blast page)

features.description: Neck lesions are gray-brown and girdle the neck, causing the neck and panicle to fall over. Node blast and neck blast often occur together and look similar
features.source_name: IRRI Rice Knowledge Bank, "Blast (node and neck)" (IRRI-Node/neck blast)
features.location_in_source: "What it does" paragraph 2; "How to identify" bullet 4

features.description: Rotten-neck symptoms start at the node at the base of the panicle. Tissue browns and shrivels, so the stem breaks and lodges. If the panicle does not drop it turns white to gray, or unfilled florets turn gray
features.short_quote: "Rotten neck symptoms appear at the base of the panicle"
features.source_name: LSU AgCenter Pub. 3153 "Blast of Rice" (Groth & Hollier, 6/10) (LSU-Blast)

features.description: Infection at the panicle base causes rotten neck and the panicle drops
features.source_name: Sri Lanka Department of Agriculture, Rice Research & Development Institute, Rice blast page (DOA-SriLanka)

features.description: Panicles affected by panicle blast become empty (unfilled)
features.source_name: RDA National Crop Pest Management System, paddy rice panicle blast (NCPMS-Panicle blast; text identical to the leaf blast page)

features.description: If the neck is infected before the milk stage, no grain forms; infection afterwards produces poor-quality grain. Node and neck blast produce whiteheads like stem borers. Stem-borer whiteheads pull out easily, but blast whiteheads do not
features.short_quote: "tugging on the stem will not result in removal"
features.source_name: IRRI Rice Knowledge Bank, "Blast (node and neck)" (IRRI-Node/neck blast)
features.location_in_source: "How to identify" bullet 5 and lower bullets

features.description: Gray-brown lesions form at the branching joints of panicle branches and floret stalks
features.source_name: LSU AgCenter Pub. 3153 "Blast of Rice" (Groth & Hollier, 6/10) (LSU-Blast)

features.description: In severe cases secondary panicle branches and grains are also attacked, producing partly filled grains ('whiteheads')
features.source_name: Sri Lanka Department of Agriculture, Rice Research & Development Institute, Rice blast page (DOA-SriLanka)

features.description: Acute-type leaf lesions; under high humidity gray mold (conidia) appears on the surface of the neck, panicle branches and nodes
features.source_name: RDA National Crop Pest Management System, paddy rice leaf blast (NCPMS-Leaf blast)

features.description: The pathogen spreads by spores carried by wind and rain (Figure 1 spore photo)
features.source_name: LSU AgCenter Pub. 3153 "Blast of Rice" (Groth & Hollier, 6/10) (LSU-Blast)

features.description: Because of seed-borne inoculum, leaf lesions also form in the nursery. In the paddy field it occurs mainly from late June and leads on to panicle blast. Panicle blast infection occurs around heading, and the main inoculum is thought to be leaf-blast lesions on the upper leaves
features.growth_stage: Seedling raising; paddy field from late June; around heading
features.source_name: RDA National Crop Pest Management System, paddy rice leaf blast (NCPMS-Leaf blast)

features.description: Occurs at all growth stages, but leaf blast declines once plants mature and acquire adult-plant resistance
features.source_name: IRRI Rice Knowledge Bank, "Blast (leaf and collar)" (IRRI-Leaf/collar blast)

features.description: Found from seedling to maturity. The leaf blast phase is seedling to late tillering, and neck blast occurs at heading (US basis)
features.source_name: LSU AgCenter Pub. 3153 "Blast of Rice" (Groth & Hollier, 6/10) (LSU-Blast)

features.description: Severe in years with frequent rain and low summer temperatures during the growing season, especially with cold damage. Frequent rain and gloomy, humid weather around heading cause major panicle blast outbreaks. Heavy nitrogen application makes it worse
features.source_name: RDA National Crop Pest Management System, paddy rice leaf blast (NCPMS-Leaf blast)

features.description: Occurrence increases with low night temperatures (17–20 °C), high humidity, excess nitrogen, foggy and cloudy weather, and dense planting
features.source_name: Sri Lanka Department of Agriculture, Rice Research & Development Institute, Rice blast page (DOA-SriLanka)

features.description: Belongs to the ascomycetes (perfect state), but the conidial state is usual in the field. Conidia are colorless, pear-shaped, with 2 septa, 14–37 × 5–12 µm. On media it forms dark-brown globose perithecia and spindle-shaped ascospores
features.short_quote: "conidia are colorless, pear-shaped, with two septa" (translated from Korean)
features.source_name: RDA National Crop Pest Management System, paddy rice leaf blast (NCPMS-Leaf blast)

features.description: Genus *Pyricularia* characters: conidia are solitary, pyriform to obclavate, narrowing toward the tip with a rounded base, 2-septate, colorless to pale brown, with a distinct basal hilum. Conidiophores are brown and grow sympodially, and conidia detach rhexolytically. Ascospores are colorless, fusiform, curved, with 3 transverse septa
features.short_quote: "pyriform to obclavate, narrowed toward tip, rounded at the base, 2-septate"
features.source_name: Klaubauf S. et al. 2014. Studies in Mycology 79:85–120, "Pyriculariaceae" phylogenetic paper (Klaubauf 2014)

features.description: The *P. oryzae* Cavara entry in the same paper gives only a list of examined specimens and a figure (Fig. 15: sporulation on barley seed on SNA, conidiophores and conidia, scale bar 10 µm) and no conidial size figures (Unconfirmed). Its specimen list includes isolates from weeds and grasses (*Festuca*, *Lolium*, *Phleum*, *Panicum miliaceum*) in Suwon and Yongin, Korea
features.source_name: Klaubauf S. et al. 2014. Studies in Mycology 79:85–120, "Pyriculariaceae" phylogenetic paper (Klaubauf 2014)

features.description: The pathogen grows at 8–37 °C with an optimum of 25–28 °C. Conidia form at 12–34 °C, and the optimum for sporulation is the same as for growth
features.source_name: RDA National Crop Pest Management System, paddy rice leaf blast (NCPMS-Leaf blast)

source_conflicts: Leaf lesion border color differs between sources: NCPMS gives 'red' for the chronic type, IRRI 'red to brown or necrotic', LSU 'narrow brown', and the Sri Lanka Department of Agriculture 'brown, reddish-brown or yellowish-brown'. For early spots, IRRI describes white to gray-green with dark green borders, while LSU describes white, gray or bluish.

Lesion size (1.0–1.5 × 0.3–0.5 cm) appears only in the Sri Lanka Department of Agriculture page, with no original source cited. NCPMS, IRRI and LSU give no size, so this figure must not be used as if it were a Korean standard.
Node lesion color is dark brown in NCPMS, black to gray-brown (banded) in IRRI, and black rot in Sri Lanka; neck color is light brown in NCPMS and gray-brown in IRRI.
Only NCPMS explicitly mentions gray mold (signs) on lesions.

Conidial size 14–37 × 5–12 µm appears only in NCPMS and could not be cross-checked. Color also differs: NCPMS says 'colorless' while the Klaubauf 2014 genus description says 'colorless to pale brown', and the Klaubauf 2014 *P. oryzae* entry gives no size.
The NCPMS leaf blast and panicle blast pages have character-for-character identical pathogen, environment and symptom text, so they cannot count as two independent sources.
Scientific names differ (NCPMS *Magnaporthe grisea*, LSU *Pyricularia grisea*). Klaubauf 2014 separates *P. oryzae* and *P. grisea* as distinct species.
Timing is given by the Korean calendar in NCPMS (paddy field from late June; around heading) and by US growth stages in LSU (leaf blast from seedling to late tillering; neck blast at heading).
diseases.photo_visible: Spindle-shaped lesions pointed at both ends (grayish-white center, brownish border), browning and breaking of nodes and necks, whiteheads that do not pull out (pull test), gray mold under humid conditions.
diseases.lab_required: Pear shape, 2 septa and size of conidia (microscopy), definitive separation from early brown spot lesions, species-level identification (*P. oryzae* vs *P. grisea*, molecular).

diseases.intro: There is a Korean official description (NCPMS) and an original paper on anastomosis groups of Korean isolates (Kim 1994), but lesion and sclerotium sizes differ greatly between sources.

features.description: Initially, water-soaked oval lesions that look blanched form on the leaf sheath; they enlarge as dark green lesions and the surrounding area turns light brown. Lesion size is not uniform
features.short_quote: "water-soaked oval lesions, as if blanched" (translated from Korean)
features.source_name: NCPMS paddy rice Sheath blight (NCPMS-Sheath blight)

features.description: Oval to oblong gray-green lesions form on the leaf sheath, usually 1–3 cm long. In flooded fields they first appear just above the soil or water surface
features.short_quote: "usually 1-3 cm long, on the leaf sheath"

features.description: Large oval spots form on the leaf sheath. Lesions about 0.5–1 cm wide and 1–3 cm long form slightly above the water line on infected stems. Lesion centers are grayish-white or light green, with brown to reddish-brown borders
features.short_quote: "about 0.5 - 1 cm in width and 1 - 3 cm in length"
features.growth_stage: Infection begins from late tillering to internode elongation
features.source_name: LSU AgCenter Pub. 3123 "Sheath Blight of Rice" (2 pages) (LSU-SB)

features.description: Starts as small water-soaked oval or irregular lesions near the water line on lower leaf sheaths, light green or gray in color. Lesions enlarge and merge into large irregular blotches girdling the sheath. Old lesions have tan to light-brown centers with distinct dark green or brown borders
features.source_name: University of Arkansas FSA7583 "Rice Sheath Blight" (Nicolli, Dalla Lana, Pedrozo, Ronning; PDF dated 2025-08) (UAEX-SB)
features.location_in_source: "Symptoms" Initial Symptoms and Lesion Development bullets (Fig. 3A–C)

features.description: Leaf lesions are usually irregular; with age the center becomes grayish-white and the margin brown

Irregular spots form on the leaf blade. When sheath lesions merge, the leaf blade turns yellow-orange and eventually dies. The LSU photo gallery describes leaf lesions as 'snakeskin-like' (gallery caption text Unconfirmed; seen only in a search snippet)
features.source_name: LSU AgCenter Pub. 3123 "Sheath Blight of Rice" (2 pages) (LSU-SB)

features.description: In highly susceptible cultivars the fungus spreads into the culm from early sheath infection. Infected culms weaken and tillers lodge or collapse
features.source_name: LSU AgCenter Pub. 3123 "Sheath Blight of Rice" (2 pages) (LSU-SB)

features.description: Infected leaves senesce and die quickly, and young tillers also die. As a result canopy leaf area falls and yield declines
Severely affected plants show early leaf senescence, fewer tillers and poor grain filling
features.source_name: University of Arkansas FSA7583 "Rice Sheath Blight" (Nicolli, Dalla Lana, Pedrozo, Ronning; PDF dated 2025-08) (UAEX-SB)

features.description: As the rice grows, lesions gradually move upward. Secondary spread happens when mycelium from sheath lesions forms new lesions on neighboring stems, hills and leaves
features.plant_part: Leaf sheath to leaves and adjacent hills
features.source_name: NCPMS paddy rice Sheath blight (NCPMS-Sheath blight)

features.description: Under favorable conditions early lesions multiply and enlarge, moving up the sheath and onto the leaves. They then spread to tillers of neighboring hills (transplanted) or neighboring plants (direct-seeded)
features.plant_part: Leaf sheath to leaves to adjacent hills

features.description: Lower leaf sheaths and blades are attacked at internode elongation. After panicle emergence, disease progresses quickly up to the flag leaf in susceptible cultivars. The fungus does not form spores and spreads by growing from hill to hill, so it appears as circular patches in the field
features.short_quote: "Infected plants are usually found in a circular pattern"
features.source_name: LSU AgCenter Pub. 3123 "Sheath Blight of Rice" (2 pages) (LSU-SB)

features.description: The disease progresses in two phases. In the vertical phase, sclerotia or debris infect the tiller base at the water line and move up into the canopy; in the horizontal phase, mycelium spreads hill to hill by physical contact with healthy tissue. In severe cases stems weaken and lodge early. Cultivar susceptibility increases after heading
features.source_name: University of Arkansas FSA7583 "Rice Sheath Blight" (Nicolli, Dalla Lana, Pedrozo, Ronning; PDF dated 2025-08) (UAEX-SB)

features.description: Sclerotia are mycelial masses of irregular size and shape, but most are brown and round, about 1–2 mm. The fungus overwinters as sclerotia, which attach to leaf sheaths after transplanting and cause disease
features.short_quote: "mostly brown, round, about 1-2 mm" (translated from Korean)
features.growth_stage: Formed late July to early August
features.source_name: NCPMS paddy rice Sheath blight (NCPMS-Sheath blight)
features.location_in_source: Pathogen information > pathogen characteristics; symptom description sentence 2

features.description: Sclerotia are white at first and turn brown to black as they mature. They can be 6 mm or more in diameter and float when fields are flooded. They survive in soil for more than 2 years. Laboratory formation stages are (A) white mycelial tangle → (B) differentiation to yellow-light brown → (C) brown, with visible droplets → (D) black, dry mature sclerotium
features.short_quote: "They can be 6 mm or more in diameter"
features.growth_stage: Late disease development, end of season
features.source_name: University of Arkansas FSA7583 "Rice Sheath Blight" (Nicolli, Dalla Lana, Pedrozo, Ronning; PDF dated 2025-08) (UAEX-SB)

features.description: Under high humidity, cottony white mycelium is often seen on the surface of infected sheaths
features.short_quote: "Cottony white fungal mycelium"
features.source_name: University of Arkansas FSA7583 "Rice Sheath Blight" (Nicolli, Dalla Lana, Pedrozo, Ronning; PDF dated 2025-08) (UAEX-SB)

features.description: Sclerotia are tightly interwoven mycelial masses covered by an impermeable, hydrophobic layer secreted by the fungus. They form on lesion surfaces of weedy grasses, rice and soybean
features.source_name: LSU AgCenter Pub. 3123 "Sheath Blight of Rice" (2 pages) (LSU-SB)

features.description: In subtropical environments disease is mainly started by sclerotia, and diseased crops produce up to 2 million sclerotia per m². The role of sclerotia in the tropics is uncertain. The fungus does not produce airborne spores and spreads by mycelium growing over plant tissue
features.short_quote: "does not produce aerially dispersed spores"

features.description: Resembles stem rot and stem-borer damage. Confirm by irregular sheath lesions (water-soaked to gray-green early, grayish-white with brown border later) and the presence of sclerotia
Overwintering sclerotia float to the water surface during puddling and attach between leaves and sheaths after transplanting. Most sclerotia form from late July to early August
features.source_name: NCPMS paddy rice Sheath blight (NCPMS-Sheath blight)
features.location_in_source: Disease environment sentence 1; symptom description sentence 2

features.description: Symptoms are usually observed from tillering to the milk stage
features.short_quote: "from tillering to milk stage"

features.description: Infection usually begins from late tillering to internode elongation
features.source_name: LSU AgCenter Pub. 3123 "Sheath Blight of Rice" (2 pages) (LSU-SB)

features.description: Infection can occur at any growth stage but is most common after tillering. Symptoms appear from tillering to booting and progress quickly under hot, humid conditions
features.source_name: University of Arkansas FSA7583 "Rice Sheath Blight" (Nicolli, Dalla Lana, Pedrozo, Ronning; PDF dated 2025-08) (UAEX-SB)

features.description: Infection is possible at 22–35 °C, optimum 30–32 °C. Disease is heavy when humidity between hills stays at 96% or above. Excess nitrogen, dense planting, cropping season and cultivar affect it
features.source_name: NCPMS paddy rice Sheath blight (NCPMS-Sheath blight)

features.description: Occurs with high temperature (28–32 °C), high nitrogen fertilization and canopy relative humidity of 85–100%. More prevalent in the rainy season
Favored by 73–95 °F (about 22.8–35 °C), optimum 86–90 °F (about 30–32.2 °C), and relative humidity above 95%
features.source_name: University of Arkansas FSA7583 "Rice Sheath Blight" (Nicolli, Dalla Lana, Pedrozo, Ronning; PDF dated 2025-08) (UAEX-SB)

features.description: Under the microscope the hyphae consist of long multinucleate cells with septa. They branch at 90° from the main hypha with a constriction at the branch point and a septum just above the branch. Hyphae are colorless. Sexual spores are produced but rarely observed in Arkansas fields
features.short_quote: "branching at 90° angles to the main hyphae with constriction"
features.source_name: University of Arkansas FSA7583 "Rice Sheath Blight" (Nicolli, Dalla Lana, Pedrozo, Ronning; PDF dated 2025-08) (UAEX-SB)

features.description: The causal agent is *R. solani* AG1-IA. An AG (anastomosis group) is defined by the ability of genetically similar isolates to fuse hyphae and is used for identification. AG11 and AG4 cause seedling damping-off but not sheath blight
features.source_name: University of Arkansas FSA7583 "Rice Sheath Blight" (Nicolli, Dalla Lana, Pedrozo, Ronning; PDF dated 2025-08) (UAEX-SB)

features.description: 2,276 *R. solani* isolates from 68 crops in Korea were divided by anastomosis testing into AG-1 (1,091 isolates), AG-2-1, AG-2-2, AG-3, AG-4 and AG-5. Of AG-1, 791 isolates were cultural type IA, and IA was isolated from 7 crops. The optimum mycelial growth temperature of AG-1 is 26–30 °C, and the minimum for AG-1 (IA) is 10–11 °C. At 26 °C, AG-1 (IA) and (IB) grew fastest after AG-1 (IC). The abstract does not name the 7 crops yielding IA, so whether rice isolates were IA cannot be confirmed from this abstract alone (Unconfirmed)
features.source_name: Kim W.G., Cho W.D., Lee Y.H. 1994. Korean Journal of Mycology 22(4):309–324, "Anastomosis Groups and Cultural Characteristics of *Rhizoctonia solani* Isolates from Crops in Korea" (Kim 1994)

source_conflicts: Sclerotium size is the biggest discrepancy. NCPMS says 'mostly brown and round, about 1–2 mm', while UAEX (USA) says 'can reach 6 mm or more in diameter, white turning brown to black'. IRRI and LSU give no size.
Lesion size is 1–3 cm long in IRRI and 0.5–1 cm wide × 1–3 cm long in LSU; NCPMS gives no figure ('size not uniform').

Lesion color: NCPMS dark green with surrounding light brown; IRRI grayish-white center with brown margin; LSU grayish-white or light green center with brown to reddish-brown border; UAEX tan to light-brown center with dark green or brown border.

Timing: IRRI tillering to milk stage, UAEX tillering to booting, LSU infection starting late tillering to internode elongation; NCPMS gives calendar dates such as sclerotium formation in late July to early August.
Humidity thresholds differ: NCPMS 96% or above, UAEX above 95%, IRRI 85–100%. Temperatures are effectively the same: NCPMS 22–35 °C (optimum 30–32 °C) and UAEX 73–95 °F.
The AG1-IA designation appears only in UAEX. The Kim 1994 abstract only says AG-1 IA was isolated from 7 crops, so whether rice isolates were IA is Unconfirmed at the abstract level.
On spores, IRRI and LSU say 'no airborne spores', while UAEX says sexual spores form but are rare in the field.
diseases.photo_visible: Oval gray-green sheath lesions with brown borders just above the water line, upward progression, circular patches in the field, brown sclerotia and cottony white mycelium under humid conditions.
diseases.lab_required: 90° hyphal branching with constriction at the branch point (microscopy), AG1-IA determination (anastomosis test, culture), definitive separation from similar diseases such as stem rot.

diseases.intro: There is a Korean official source (NCPMS) and an original paper on 50 Korean isolates (Kim 2025); the conidial sizes in the two sources differ greatly.

features.description: Early lesions have a dark-brown oval necrotic area surrounded by a yellow toxic zone (halo). Over time they become large round lesions with concentric rings
features.short_quote: "yellow toxic zone around dark-brown oval necrotic area" (translated from Korean)
features.growth_stage: Not stated (lower leaves more prone to infection)
features.source_name: NCPMS paddy rice Brown spot (NCPMS-Brown spot)

features.description: Leaf lesions appear from tillering. At first they are small, round, dark-brown to purple-brown spots
Fully developed lesions are round to oval with light-brown to gray centers and reddish-brown borders. IRRI states that the reddish-brown border is caused by a toxin produced by the fungus
features.short_quote: "reddish brown margin caused by the toxin"

features.description: On susceptible cultivars lesions are 5–14 mm long and leaves may wilt. On resistant cultivars lesions are brown and pinhead-sized
features.short_quote: "On resistant varieties, the lesions are brown and pinhead-sized."

features.description: On some cultivars it can be mistaken for blast lesions. Confirm by round brown spots with gray centers surrounded by reddish-brown borders
The most conspicuous damage is the many large spots on leaves, which can kill the whole leaf

Infected seedlings develop small, round, yellow-brown or brown lesions. Lesions can girdle the coleoptile and distort the first and second leaves. Heavily infected seed causes seedling blight, killing 10–58% of seedlings
features.location_in_source: "How to identify" first bullet; "Why is it important"

features.description: Stems basically show fine dark-brown markings. Later these enlarge and merge so the whole stem turns pale brown. Panicle stalks develop dark-brown streaks and later turn entirely dark brown
features.source_name: NCPMS paddy rice Brown spot (NCPMS-Brown spot)

features.description: Leaf sheath lesions resemble leaf lesions
features.location_in_source: "How to identify" paragraph below the photo

features.description: Grains develop dark-brown spots that later become grayish-white collapsed areas. Often the whole grain surface browns. Unlike blast, it does not attack quickly from the panicle tip and does not cause whiteheads
features.short_quote: "does not cause whiteheads as blast does" (translated from Korean)
features.growth_stage: Grains are more prone to infection the closer to heading
features.source_name: NCPMS paddy rice Brown spot (NCPMS-Brown spot)

features.description: Infected glumes and panicle branches show dark-brown to black oval spots or discoloration of the whole surface. Infected florets fill incompletely and quality falls. The fungus penetrates grains, producing spotted, discolored grain ('pecky rice'). Seed infection produces unfilled or spotted, discolored seed
features.location_in_source: "How to identify" 2 paragraphs below the photo; "What it does"

features.description: In September 2023, brown spot lesions appeared on leaves, necks and panicles of rice in Gimje and Gunsan, Jeonbuk, and were collected intensively. Isolates were also obtained from leaf lesions in Jangheung (Jeonnam), Sancheong, Sacheon and Goseong (Gyeongnam) and Gyeongju (Gyeongbuk), and in 2024 two isolates came from leaves in Suncheon, Jeonnam (collected in July and August)
features.source_name: Kim S., Chung H., Jang S.-H. et al. 2025. Plant Pathology Journal 41(5):671–681, doi 10.5423/PPJ.FT.08.2025.0106, RAPD and mycological traits of 50 Korean *B. oryzae* isolates (Kim 2025)

features.description: On secondary signs: the NCPMS original says lesions do not form conidia, and that healthy tissue around the lesion dies and forms conidia from the start. The meaning of the sentence is ambiguous, so it is kept as in the original
features.source_name: NCPMS paddy rice Brown spot (NCPMS-Brown spot)

features.description: Disease occurs throughout the growing period but rises sharply in the paddy field after panicle initiation. Lower leaves are more prone, and grains are more prone closer to heading. Stems, panicles, panicle stalks and panicle branches become more prone as days after heading increase. The last panicle infection affecting yield is up to 25 days after heading. Conidia trapped 80 cm above ground are few from booting to the dough stage and increase sharply near harvest
features.short_quote: "last panicle infection affecting yield is up to 25 days after heading" (translated from Korean)
features.growth_stage: From panicle initiation to 25 days after heading
features.source_name: NCPMS paddy rice Brown spot (NCPMS-Brown spot)

features.description: Can occur at all growth stages, but infection from maximum tillering to grain filling is most important. Infection requires 8–24 hours of leaf wetness and occurs at 86–100% RH and 16–36 °C
features.short_quote: "most critical during maximum tillering up to the ripening stages"

features.description: In Korea brown spot normally occurs at harvest, but interest has grown because its timing has recently shifted. Incidence in 2001–2008 was 30–50% (introduction; original source in the paper's references)
features.source_name: Kim S., Chung H., Jang S.-H. et al. 2025. Plant Pathology Journal 41(5):671–681, doi 10.5423/PPJ.FT.08.2025.0106, RAPD and mycological traits of 50 Korean *B. oryzae* isolates (Kim 2025)

features.description: Optimum temperature for conidial germination is 20–30 °C, with 90% germinating in 3 hours. Infection needs air humidity of 70% at flowering and 90% at the dough stage. Unlike the blast fungus, conidia rarely fly at night; they fly mostly from 08–09 h to 15 h, and field spore counts peak near maturity
features.source_name: NCPMS paddy rice Brown spot (NCPMS-Brown spot)

features.description: Conidia are nearly cylindrical, usually curved, pale brown to yellow-brown, with 6–14 septa, 63–153 µm long and 14–22 µm wide. They germinate from one or both end cells. Conidiophores are septate, about 600 µm long and 4–8 µm wide
features.short_quote: "has 6-14 septa and is 63-153 µm long" (translated from Korean)
features.source_name: NCPMS paddy rice Brown spot (NCPMS-Brown spot)

features.description: The original says the 'ascus' is dark brown, globose to elliptical, 360–780 µm in diameter. It then again says the 'ascus' is clavate to cylindrical-clavate, 21–26 µm wide and 140–235 µm long. Ascospores are 235–648 µm long and 4–9 µm wide, filiform with 8–12 septa and a mucilaginous sheath, coiled helically within the ascus
features.source_name: NCPMS paddy rice Brown spot (NCPMS-Brown spot)

features.description: For 6 representative Korean isolates (14 days on PDA), conidia ranged 27.4–96.3 µm long and 6.0–19.8 µm wide. Isolate means ranged from 53.1 × 11.2 µm (F1305) to 75.0 × 15.2 µm (F1371), based on at least 2 experiments per isolate and 50 measurements per experiment. In slide culture, 2–4 conidia were borne per conidiophore. Septum numbers were not reported (Unconfirmed)
features.source_name: Kim S., Chung H., Jang S.-H. et al. 2025. Plant Pathology Journal 41(5):671–681, doi 10.5423/PPJ.FT.08.2025.0106, RAPD and mycological traits of 50 Korean *B. oryzae* isolates (Kim 2025)
features.location_in_source: Results mycological traits paragraph; Table 3 and footnotes

features.description: At 25 °C on PDA all isolates grew fast, forming cottony colonies 45–70 mm in diameter in 90 mm Petri dishes within 5 days. The upper side mostly has a gray cottony center, with white margins in some isolates (F1253, F1371). The reverse is dark gray to almost black
features.source_name: Kim S., Chung H., Jang S.-H. et al. 2025. Plant Pathology Journal 41(5):671–681, doi 10.5423/PPJ.FT.08.2025.0106, RAPD and mycological traits of 50 Korean *B. oryzae* isolates (Kim 2025)

features.description: ITS sequences of all 50 isolates were identical and matched *B. oryzae* CBS 199.54 at 100% (562/562 bp). RAPD divided them into 5 groups (group A 84%). Lesions were observed 1 day after inoculation (30 °C, 80–90% humidity) (seedling inoculation conditions)
features.source_name: Kim S., Chung H., Jang S.-H. et al. 2025. Plant Pathology Journal 41(5):671–681, doi 10.5423/PPJ.FT.08.2025.0106, RAPD and mycological traits of 50 Korean *B. oryzae* isolates (Kim 2025)
features.location_in_source: Methods pathogenicity test; Results ITS paragraph

features.description: Produces the non-host-specific toxin ophiobolin
features.source_name: NCPMS paddy rice Brown spot (NCPMS-Brown spot)

source_conflicts: Conidial size differs most. NCPMS gives 63–153 × 14–22 µm (6–14 septa), while Kim 2025 measured 27.4–96.3 × 6.0–19.8 µm (means 53–75 µm) for 6 Korean isolates on PDA. This may reflect spores from media versus lesions, but neither source explains it.
Lesion size figures (5–14 mm on susceptible, pinhead-sized on resistant) appear only in IRRI. Concentric rings appear only in NCPMS.

Halo descriptions differ. NCPMS describes a 'yellow toxic zone' on early lesions, while the IRRI brown spot page describes a 'reddish-brown border caused by toxin'. The yellow halo appears in the differentiation paragraph of the IRRI blast page.
The NCPMS sexual-stage description mentions 'ascus' twice with different sizes. The first (360–780 µm diameter, globose) appears to be an error for perithecium (inference in the notes).
The NCPMS disease-environment sentence 'lesions do not form conidia…' is ambiguous.

Timing: NCPMS says sharp rise after panicle initiation and panicle infection up to 25 days after heading; IRRI says maximum tillering to grain filling; Kim 2025 says typically at harvest but with a recent shift in timing (isolates from July–August 2024).
Seedling symptoms (girdling the coleoptile, 10–58% seedling death) appear only in IRRI.
diseases.photo_visible: Round to oval brown lesions (gray or light-brown center, reddish-brown border, yellow halo), dark-brown spots or overall browning of grains, and no whiteheads.
diseases.lab_required: Conidial shape, septa and size (microscopy; figures vary widely between sources), ITS and RAPD identification (molecular), ophiobolin toxin (biochemical).

diseases.intro: Descriptions from three sources (NCPMS in Korea, IRRI, EPPO) largely agree; comparison rows for bacterial blight taken from the bacterial leaf streak notes are also included in this table.

features.description: Paddy-field symptoms after peak tillering start on mature lower leaves. In the original wording, small water-soaked lesions form on 'the leaf margin 5–6 cm below the leaf blade' (whether the reference point is the leaf tip is unclear in the original)
features.source_name: NCPMS paddy rice Bacterial blight (NCPMS-Bacterial blight)

features.description: Lesions usually enlarge after 2–3 days, turning yellow to yellow-orange and spreading up and down as well as widening. The boundary with healthy tissue is water-soaked. They start from one or both leaf margins and spread to the leaf center, forming wavy-edged lesions. Over time they fade from yellowish-white to white or grayish-white and become dirty-colored due to secondary colonizers
features.short_quote: "enlarges into wavy-edged lesions" (translated from Korean)
features.source_name: NCPMS paddy rice Bacterial blight (NCPMS-Bacterial blight)

features.description: On mature plants it usually appears as water-soaked to yellow-orange stripes on the leaf blade, leaf tip or mechanical wounds. Lesion margins are wavy and progress toward the leaf base
features.short_quote: "Lesions have a wavy margin and progress toward the leaf base."
features.location_in_source: "How to identify" Check for lesions, first bullet

features.description: Old lesions turn yellow to grayish-white, and black dots appear as various saprophytes grow. On severely affected leaves lesions can extend to the leaf sheath
features.location_in_source: "How to identify" paragraph below the ooze photo

features.description: Appears as light green to gray-green water-soaked stripes near the tips and margins of young plants after transplanting. Later lesions merge into yellowish-white with wavy margins, and eventually the whole leaf turns white or gray and dies
features.short_quote: "pale-green to grey-green water-soaked streaks near the leaf tip and margins"
features.growth_stage: Young plants after transplanting to late stage
features.source_name: EPPO Global Database, *X. oryzae* pv. *oryzae* datasheet (BIOLOGY 2022-06-03, DETECTION AND IDENTIFICATION 2022-06-16) (EPPO-XANTOR)

features.description: Symptoms appear mainly on leaf blades and leaf sheaths
features.source_name: NCPMS paddy rice Bacterial blight (NCPMS-Bacterial blight)

features.description: In more susceptible cultivars, leaf sheaths and culms can also be attacked
features.source_name: EPPO Global Database, *X. oryzae* pv. *oryzae* datasheet (BIOLOGY 2022-06-03, DETECTION AND IDENTIFICATION 2022-06-16) (EPPO-XANTOR)

features.description: Symptoms sometimes also appear on grains
features.source_name: NCPMS paddy rice Bacterial blight (NCPMS-Bacterial blight)

features.description: Gray to light-brown lesions can form on the glumes of the panicle, which can lead to sterility or reduced grain quality
features.source_name: EPPO Global Database, *X. oryzae* pv. *oryzae* datasheet (BIOLOGY 2022-06-03, DETECTION AND IDENTIFICATION 2022-06-16) (EPPO-XANTOR)

features.description: Infection at booting does not affect yield but lowers grain quality and increases the proportion of broken grains

Late in the nursery, small water-soaked lesions appear on lower leaves, and dried beads of bacterial exudate form on the surface. A few days later they turn yellow, dry white from the tip, and the leaf dies rapidly
features.source_name: NCPMS paddy rice Bacterial blight (NCPMS-Bacterial blight)

features.description: From about 20–30 days after transplanting until peak tillering, seedlings suddenly dry up and die. There are no distinct symptoms, but beads smaller than millet grains are visible on leaf margins or tips. This does not occur after peak tillering. It is a wilt caused by the pathogen multiplying at the base and blocking the vessels
features.short_quote: "characteristically does not occur after peak tillering" (translated from Korean)
features.growth_stage: 20-30 days after transplanting to peak tillering
features.source_name: NCPMS paddy rice Bacterial blight (NCPMS-Bacterial blight)

features.description: In seedlings, infected leaves turn gray-green and roll. As the disease progresses, leaves turn yellow to straw-colored and wilt, and the whole seedling dries and dies

Systemic infection ('kresek') occurs in young plants or tillering plants of highly susceptible cultivars, causing leaves to dry, wilt and die. It is particularly severe in young transplanted plants. Larger plants may have leaves that yellow, wilt and die, and surviving plants are yellow and stunted. Clipping leaves at transplanting is an effective route for kresek spread (pale yellow leaves, severe wilting, frequent death)
features.source_name: EPPO Global Database, *X. oryzae* pv. *oryzae* datasheet (BIOLOGY 2022-06-03, DETECTION AND IDENTIFICATION 2022-06-16) (EPPO-XANTOR)

features.description: When morning dew forms, pale milky dew droplets appear on the lesion surface and dry into yellow beads. These beads fall onto the water surface with wind and become secondary inoculum
features.short_quote: "pale milky dew forms and dries into yellow beads" (translated from Korean)
features.source_name: NCPMS paddy rice Bacterial blight (NCPMS-Bacterial blight)

features.description: On young lesions, bacterial ooze resembling milky dew drops is visible in the early morning. The ooze later dries into small yellow beads on the underside of the leaf
features.short_quote: "bacterial ooze resembling a milky dew drop"
features.location_in_source: "How to identify" Check for lesions, bullet 2

features.description: Bacterial ooze may be seen on water-soaked stripes in the early morning. Multiplied bacteria are exuded as slimy droplets and re-enter through hydathodes
features.source_name: EPPO Global Database, *X. oryzae* pv. *oryzae* datasheet (BIOLOGY 2022-06-03, DETECTION AND IDENTIFICATION 2022-06-16) (EPPO-XANTOR)

features.description: To tell kresek from stem-borer damage, squeeze the lower part of an infected seedling between the fingers. With kresek, yellow bacterial ooze comes out of the cut surface, and unlike stem-borer-damaged plants it does not pull out easily. For leaves, cut across a young lesion, place it in a clear container of clean water, and after a few minutes hold it to the light to see whether turbid liquid streams from the cut end
features.location_in_source: "How to identify" kresek paragraph, last "To quickly diagnose" bullet

features.description: Usually develops around heading, but in chronic and heavily affected areas it develops early in the paddy field and rarely even in the nursery. The number of rainy days and rainfall from late July to late August are important. Major outbreaks occur with July mean temperature 22–24 °C, July rainfall of 200 mm or more and wind speed of 15 m/s or more; incidence was 8.8% after 12 hours of submergence and 72.7% after 48 hours
features.source_name: NCPMS paddy rice Bacterial blight (NCPMS-Bacterial blight)

features.description: In temperate regions it is usually observed late in the nursery (citing Ou 1985). In both temperate and tropical regions, 25–34 °C, RH above 70%, strong winds and frequent heavy rain (typhoons) favor disease (citing Mew et al. 1993)
features.source_name: EPPO Global Database, *X. oryzae* pv. *oryzae* datasheet (BIOLOGY 2022-06-03, DETECTION AND IDENTIFICATION 2022-06-16) (EPPO-XANTOR)

features.description: Occurs readily at 25–34 °C and RH above 70%. It spreads by ooze droplets during strong winds and continuous heavy rain. The earlier it occurs, the greater the yield loss
features.location_in_source: "Why and where it occurs"; "Why is it important"

features.description: A bacterial vascular disease. Cells are rods 1–2 × 0.8 µm with rounded ends and a single terminal flagellum. The original gives the flagellum as '30μ thick and 8.75μ long' (units as written). Gram-negative, no spores. The surface is covered by sticky polysaccharide slime (capsule)
features.source_name: NCPMS paddy rice Bacterial blight (NCPMS-Bacterial blight)

features.description: Aerobic, motile, Gram-negative rod. Non-spore-forming and capsulated, occurring singly or in pairs, 1.1–2.0 × 0.4–0.6 µm, with one polar flagellum. It mainly attacks vascular tissue. By contrast, pv. *oryzicola* (bacterial leaf streak) attacks mesophyll parenchyma
features.short_quote: "1.1-2.0 x 0.4-0.6 µm in size, with one polar flagellum"
features.source_name: EPPO Global Database, *X. oryzae* pv. *oryzae* datasheet (BIOLOGY 2022-06-03, DETECTION AND IDENTIFICATION 2022-06-16) (EPPO-XANTOR)
features.location_in_source: DETECTION AND IDENTIFICATION > Morphology; BIOLOGY sentence 1

features.description: Grows relatively slowly, but forms yellow, round, smooth colonies on nutrient media in 3–4 days. It can grow even at 5–10 °C, with an optimum of 26–30 °C. Without nutrients it survives about 20 days at 20 °C and a few days at 30 °C. It survives 8 months or more in diseased straw and on *Leersia* grass and similar hosts
features.source_name: NCPMS paddy rice Bacterial blight (NCPMS-Bacterial blight)

features.description: Isolated on PSA, NBY, GF agar or semi-selective media. After 3–7 days on NA, colonies are round, entire, smooth, convex, opaque and pale yellow to straw yellow (1–2 mm). Optimum growth temperature is 25–30 °C, and it does not survive long on solid media. Catalase positive and unable to reduce nitrate
features.short_quote: "pale to straw yellow,1-2 mm in size"
features.source_name: EPPO Global Database, *X. oryzae* pv. *oryzae* datasheet (BIOLOGY 2022-06-03, DETECTION AND IDENTIFICATION 2022-06-16) (EPPO-XANTOR)
features.location_in_source: Morphology sentences 2-5; Detection and identification methods first sentence

features.description: Enters mainly through hydathodes at leaf tips and margins, and also through stomata and wounds. After multiplying in the epithem it moves into the xylem and travels both up and down within the vessels
features.plant_part: Leaf tip and margins to xylem vessels
features.source_name: EPPO Global Database, *X. oryzae* pv. *oryzae* datasheet (BIOLOGY 2022-06-03, DETECTION AND IDENTIFICATION 2022-06-16) (EPPO-XANTOR)

features.description: Water-soaked to yellow-orange stripes form on the leaf blade, leaf tip or mechanical wounds. Margins are wavy and progress toward the leaf base. In the early morning, slime resembling milky dew forms on young lesions and dries into small yellow beads on the leaf underside.
features.short_quote: "Lesions have a wavy margin and progress toward the leaf base."

features.description: After peak tillering, small water-soaked lesions form on the leaf margin 5–6 cm below the blade tip. Pale milky dew forms during morning dew and dries into yellow beads. After 2–3 days lesions spread up and down as yellow to yellow-orange areas, forming wavy-edged lesions. Over time they change from yellowish-white to white or grayish-white.
features.short_quote: "enlarges into wavy-edged lesions" (translated from Korean)

source_conflicts: Cell size differs: NCPMS 1–2 × 0.8 µm versus EPPO 1.1–2.0 × 0.4–0.6 µm, so the width differs.

The NCPMS flagellum dimensions '30μ thick, 8.75μ long' would be thicker than the cell if read as µm, so a unit error is likely (inference in the notes). The NCPMS pathogen-name field says *X. campestris* pv. *oryzae* while its body text says *X. oryzae* pv. *oryzae*, so the naming is inconsistent within the same page.

In the NCPMS symptom description, 'the leaf margin 5–6 cm below the leaf blade' has an unclear reference point (whether the leaf tip). The comparison row from the bacterial leaf streak notes read it as '5–6 cm from the blade tip'.
Colonies: NCPMS 3–4 days, yellow; EPPO on NA 3–7 days, pale yellow to straw yellow, 1–2 mm. Optimum temperature: NCPMS 26–30 °C, EPPO 25–30 °C.
Early lesion color: IRRI water-soaked to yellow-orange; EPPO light green to gray-green water-soaked; NCPMS small water-soaked lesions turning yellow to yellow-orange after 2–3 days.

Timing differs: NCPMS (Korea) 'usually around heading' and the acute wilt type '20–30 days after transplanting to peak tillering', versus EPPO 'usually late nursery in temperate regions' (citing Ou 1985). Temperature also differs: NCPMS gives July mean temperature 22–24 °C (Korean epidemiology), IRRI and EPPO 25–34 °C.
Gray to light-brown lesions on glumes are described specifically only by EPPO.
diseases.photo_visible: Yellow-to-grayish-white lesions with wavy boundaries starting from leaf tips and margins, milky ooze in early morning and dried yellow beads, kresek seedling death, turbid streaming from cut leaves (glass-of-water test).
diseases.lab_required: Gram-negative rods with polar flagellum (microscopy), yellow colonies and biochemical reactions (culture), PCR and serological tests, separation from bacterial leaf streak (Xoc) in late-stage lesions.

diseases.intro: No Korean source confirmed. NCPMS and Nongsaro have no entry for *X. oryzae* pv. *oryzicola*, and the Korean list name 'byeo segyun-julmunui-byeong' (rice bacterial stripe) belongs to *Acidovorax avenae* subsp. *avenae*, so it is not used here (per the notes). Everything below is an overseas description.

features.description: Early symptoms are narrow, dark green, water-soaked streaks of variable length between the veins, initially only on the leaf blade. As lesions enlarge they develop yellow halos, turn yellow-orange to brown depending on cultivar, and may merge.
features.short_quote: "narrow, dark-green, water-soaked, interveinal streaks of various lengths"
features.source_name: EPPO Global Database, *X. oryzae* pv. *oryzicola* (XANTTO) Datasheet

features.description: Bacterial exudate is commonly seen on the streaks, as tiny amber droplets.
features.short_quote: "tiny amber-coloured drops"

features.description: In severe infections yellow-orange (amber) exudate emerges from stomata as small droplets. When dry, the exudate becomes small sticky beads (stalked or not). It may also dry into threads, which can be spread by dry wind.
features.short_quote: "sticky tiny beads with or without small stalks"

features.description: At advanced stages it is hard to distinguish from bacterial blight (Xoo). However, Xoc lesion margins stay straight while Xoo lesions are wavy. The two pathovars occur together in the same field and sometimes on the same plant.
features.short_quote: "lesion margins remain linear (rather than wavy…)"

features.description: In the final stage the streaks turn brown to gray and leaves may dry completely and die.
Infected florets turn brown or black, and the ovary and stamens die. Symptomatic infected seeds have browned glumes and necrotic endosperm.
features.short_quote: "browning of glumes and necrotic endosperm"

features.description: Often occurs together with feeding injury by leaf-folder larvae such as *Cnaphalocrocis medinalis* or the rice hispa (*Dicladispa armigera*), because feeding wounds let bacteria enter easily.

Enters mainly through stomata or wounds (insects, heavy rain, wind). It multiplies between mesophyll parenchyma cells (apoplast) and spreads along intercellular spaces without entering the vascular bundles. Xoo, in contrast, enters mainly through hydathodes and multiplies in the vascular bundles. This difference underlies the difference in lesion shape.
features.short_quote: "without entering the vascular tissues"

features.description: Aerobic, motile, Gram-negative rod. Non-spore-forming and capsulated, occurring singly or in pairs, 1.0–2.5 × 0.4–0.6 µm, with one polar flagellum.
features.short_quote: "1.0-2.5 x 0.4-0.6 µm in size, with one polar flagellum"

features.description: Colonies after 3 days on NA are round with smooth margins, smooth, convex and opaque, pale yellow to straw yellow, 1–2 mm. Optimum growth 25–30 °C. Because it grows slowly it is easily overgrown by fast-growing contaminants such as *Pantoea*. PSA, NBY and GF media are used for isolation, and XOS is a semi-selective medium for seed detection.
features.short_quote: "pale to straw yellow, 1-2 mm in size"

features.description: Early symptoms are small water-soaked linear lesions between the veins, initially dark green and later light brown to yellowish-gray.
features.short_quote: "small, water-soaked, linear lesions between leaf veins"
features.source_name: IRRI Rice Knowledge Bank, Bacterial leaf streak
features.location_in_source: How to identify, "Check for lesions" item 1

features.description: Lesions are translucent when held against the light. In very severe cases the whole leaf browns and dies.
features.short_quote: "translucent when held against the light"

features.description: Under humid conditions yellow droplets of bacterial exudate are visible on the leaf surface, containing masses of bacterial cells.
features.short_quote: "yellow droplets of bacterial ooze"

features.description: If the advancing part of a streak is cut and placed in a glass of water, bacterial masses stream out and the water usually becomes turbid after 5 minutes.
features.short_quote: "makes the water turbid after five minutes"
features.location_in_source: How to identify, paragraph under "To confirm"

features.description: It can be confused with narrow brown spot. Leaf streak lesions are usually narrower; narrow brown spot lesions are not translucent and have no bacterial exudate.
features.short_quote: "narrow brown spot lesions are not translucent"

features.description: In early infection, especially when lesions of both diseases are on the same leaf, bacterial blight and leaf streak look identical. Biochemical, pathogenicity and serological tests are needed to distinguish them.
features.short_quote: "Blight and streak symptoms look the same at the early stage"

features.description: Infection occurs at early stages from maximum tillering to panicle initiation. Mature plants recover easily, so yield loss is small. It occurs in hot, humid areas and carries over to the next crop through seed and infected stubble.
features.short_quote: "from maximum tillering to panicle initiation"
features.location_in_source: Why and where it occurs, paragraphs 2 and 4

features.description: Infected plants have leaves that brown and dry. In severe cases the photosynthetic area falls and grain weight decreases.
From tillering to booting, small dark green water-soaked streaks form between veins. The streaks are confined by veins and grow only lengthwise, soon turning yellow or orange-brown.
features.short_quote: "longitudinal, limited by the veins"
features.source_name: TNAU Agritech Portal, Paddy expert system: Bacterial leaf streak

features.description: Bacterial exudate is visible along the whole streak as small yellow or amber droplets.
features.short_quote: "tiny yellow or amber colored droplets"

features.description: Streaks merge into large blotches and can cover the whole leaf. In severe cases lesions turn brown to grayish-white and dry out.
Infected florets and seeds discolor brown or black, the ovary, stamens and endosperm die, and glumes brown.

Rod-shaped, without spores or capsule (EPPO says "capsulated"). One polar flagellum, Gram-negative, aerobic, grows well at 28 °C. Colonies on NA are pale yellow, round, smooth, convex, viscous and with smooth margins.
features.short_quote: "pale yellow, circular, smooth, convex, and viscid"

features.description: Narrow dark green water-soaked streaks of variable length form between the veins of the leaf blade. As lesions enlarge they turn yellow-orange to brown, and amber bacterial exudate is visible. It is hard to distinguish from bacterial blight; the main late-stage difference is the lesion margin shape (straight in leaf streak, wavy in bacterial blight).
features.short_quote: "straight in leaf streak and wavy in leaf blight"
features.source_name: Oregon State Univ. Plant Clinic (S. B. Jepson), "Bacterial leaf streak of rice" 1-page sheet (stated as reprinted from CABI Crop Protection Compendium 2005)

features.description: Enters through stomata and surface wounds (usually from insects), and bacterial masses develop in the parenchyma.
features.short_quote: "Masses of bacteria develop in the parenchyma."

features.description: In Madagascar rice fields (both upland and lowland rice, 30–80% of plants affected), water-soaked lesions developed into translucent yellow streaks with exudate visible on the surface. On inoculated leaves, water-soaked lesions with yellow exudate were reproduced after about 7 days.
features.short_quote: "translucent, yellow streaks with visible exudates"
features.source_name: Poulin L. et al. 2014, *Plant Disease* 98(10):1423 (CGSpace abstract)

features.description: Formed single yellow colonies resembling *Xanthomonas* on semi-selective PSA medium.
features.short_quote: "Single, yellow, Xanthomonas-like colonies"

features.description: Produces linear water-soaked to necrotic streaks and does not enter the vascular bundles. Distinguishing the two diseases by symptoms alone is not recommended. Amber to orange exudate serves as secondary inoculum.
features.short_quote: "Separating the two diseases based on symptoms is not recommended."
features.source_name: California Dept. of Food & Agriculture, Pest Rating Proposal: *X. oryzae* pv. *oryzicola* (comment period 2026-02-25 to 04-11)

source_conflicts: The exudate color is described differently by each source: EPPO 'amber', IRRI 'yellow', TNAU 'yellow or amber', Poulin 2014 'yellow exudate', CDFA 'amber to orange'.

Positions differ on whether it can be visually distinguished from bacterial blight. EPPO and OSU give 'straight versus wavy margins even at late stages' as the distinguishing feature, IRRI says 'they look identical early and tests are needed', and CDFA (2026) says 'distinguishing by symptoms alone is not recommended'.
Capsule statements are opposite: EPPO says 'capsulated', TNAU says 'no capsule' (unresolved; original source Unconfirmed).
The later color of early streaks is 'yellow-orange to brown' in EPPO and OSU, 'light brown to yellowish-gray' in IRRI, and 'yellow or orange-brown' in TNAU.
Infection timing differs slightly: IRRI 'maximum tillering to panicle initiation', TNAU 'tillering to booting'.
The CDFA paragraph is almost identical in wording to the EPPO BIOLOGY paragraph, so it was not counted as an independent source. The OSU material states it is reprinted from CABI CPC 2005.
diseases.photo_visible: Narrow, straight water-soaked streaks between veins (straight margins), translucent against light, yellow to amber exudate droplets, accompanying insect feeding injury.
diseases.lab_required: Definitive separation from bacterial blight (biochemical, pathogenicity, serological, PCR), colony isolation (culture); since the pathogen is not recorded in Korea, culture plus PCR is essential.

diseases.intro: The Korean official source (NCPMS) is the most detailed, and there are two Korean original papers (Kim C.K. 1981, and Niehaus 2017 on Korean isolates) plus a related news report.

features.description: Typically, seedlings grow 1.5 times or more taller than normal during the seedling-raising period and then shrivel and die within 1–2 weeks. These symptoms do not all appear at once; they occur throughout the nursery period from about 10 days after sowing.
features.short_quote: "symptoms of growing 1.5 times or more taller than normal" (translated from Korean)

features.description: Seeds heavily infected by the pathogen may show stunting in the nursery and die. Therefore, judging only by elongation, the actual rate of latent infection can be more than 10 times higher.
features.short_quote: "actual rate of latent infection is more than 10 times higher" (translated from Korean)

features.category: Symptoms - seedling/root (distinguishing from etiolated seedlings: leaf angle)
features.description: When incidence is nearly 100%, it is hard to distinguish from ordinary etiolated seedlings. In that case, if the space between the 1st and 2nd true leaves opens 45° or more as the seedling elongates, or the 2nd and 3rd leaves do not emerge, it is bakanae.
features.short_quote: "the space between the 1st and 2nd true leaves opens 45° or more" (translated from Korean)

features.category: Symptoms - seedling/root (distinguishing from etiolated seedlings: pull test)
features.description: When ordinary etiolated seedlings are pulled one by one, the stem and seed come out together. In bakanae seedlings the stem and seed separate easily.
features.short_quote: "pulled out with the stem easily separating from the seed" (translated from Korean)

features.description: Rice that showed bakanae elongation in the nursery dies within 10 days after transplanting. In the paddy field, new elongation symptoms appear as plants tiller.

From 2–3 weeks after new elongation symptoms, a white layer of mycelium and spores forms on stem sheaths. Nodes may turn pale brown, and adventitious roots often emerge from the upper nodes. In severe cases the whole hill dries and dies.
features.short_quote: "adventitious roots emerge from the upper nodes" (translated from Korean)

features.category: Symptoms - whole plant (after maximum tillering, booting)
features.description: When disease develops after maximum tillering, depending on cultivar, leaves may turn light green and stems die without elongation symptoms. Plants may also stay tall until heading and then die without heading. Hills diseased at booting rarely head, and even if they do the grain fills poorly. Tillers are few.
features.short_quote: "leaves turn light green and the stem dies" (translated from Korean)

features.description: Disease develops best at a nursery temperature of 35 °C. It also develops at around 25 °C, but there are no symptoms at 20 °C. The optimum for fungal growth is 27–30 °C. White spores on the sheaths of plants killed after maximum tillering fly to surrounding rice flowers at flowering and lie latent in the embryo and endosperm. Spores form best at 24–32 °C and decrease sharply below 20 °C and above 35 °C.
features.short_quote: "disease develops best at 35℃" (translated from Korean)

features.description: The anamorph *F. fujikuroi* produces macroconidia, microconidia and chlamydospores. Macroconidia form on sporodochia, with 3–5 septa, 36–66 × 3–3.5 µm. Microconidia are 5–12 × 2–3 µm and form chains. In the teleomorph, perithecia are globose, 250–330 × 220–280 µm, and asci are cylindrical, 90–102 × 7–9 µm, mostly with 8 ascospores (1 septum).

A seed-borne fungal disease. It enters through roots or the crown and grows systemically inside the plant. Infected plants are abnormally tall with pale, thin leaves, few tillers, and partly filled or empty grains.
features.short_quote: "abnormally tall with pale, thin leaves"

features.description: Look for seedlings in poor condition in the nursery. Infected seedlings have lesions on the roots and may die before or just after transplanting.
features.short_quote: "Infected seedlings have lesions on roots"
features.growth_stage: Nursery bed to just after transplanting

features.description: Infected plants are several inches taller and thinner than healthy plants, with yellow-green or light green leaves.
features.short_quote: "yellowish green and pale green leaves"

features.description: White powdery fungal growth appears at the base or lower part of infected plants.
features.short_quote: "white powdery growth at the base"

features.description: Roots grow from the aerial nodes of the stem.
features.short_quote: "roots growing from above-ground nodes"

features.description: Not all infected plants show elongation; they may be stunted or appear normal. Early infection kills seedlings at early tillering, and late infection produces few tillers, dry leaves, and partly filled or sterile, empty grains.
features.short_quote: "may be stunted or appear normal"

features.description: Infected seed (infection rate: Nongbaek 21%, unknown cultivar 31.7%) was raised in a wet nursery. Late in the nursery some seedlings showed typical elongation, and most leaves of these elongated seedlings died shortly after transplanting. However, the remaining stems produced abundant conidia.
features.short_quote: "most leaves of elongated nursery seedlings die within a short time" (translated from Korean)
features.growth_stage: Late wet nursery to just after transplanting
features.source_name: Kim C.K. 1981, "Studies on the occurrence ecology of rice bakanae disease" (in Korean), listed by KoreaScience as "Korean journal of applied entomology" 20(3):146–150 (published 1981-09-01)

features.description: Seedlings that looked healthy in the nursery showed typical symptoms from about 2 weeks after transplanting (mid-June) and began dying with sporulation a week later. Such diseased plants increased until mid-September. The height at which conidia formed on elongated plants rose to about 40–60% of plant height in early August. Elongated plants in early July were observed to be the main inoculum for grain infection.
features.short_quote: "seedlings carrying the pathogen that cannot be identified visually are a problem" (translated from Korean)

features.description: Seedlings infected by elongation (bakanae)-type isolates show thin, long, yellowish stems and chlorotic internodes. Gibberellin (GA) produces this phenotype. This lineage produces little or no fumonisin.
features.short_quote: "slender, elongated and yellowish stems"

features.description: With the stunting-type isolate (B14), seedling and internode lengths are smaller than or similar to the uninoculated control. Withering appears from day 5 after inoculation and intensifies on days 7 and 9. On day 9 roots are heavily colonized by mycelium and root growth is strongly inhibited. No GA is detected, while fumonisins B1 and B2 are produced in large amounts.
features.short_quote: "no GAs but high amounts of fumonisins"

features.description: Of 15 field isolates obtained in 2014–2016 from Korean rice grains and air above paddies, 9 were stunting/early-withering type and 6 were elongation type. Among 151 Korean isolates, the B14-type PCR pattern accounted for 69% of rice isolates and 85% of air isolates.

features.category: Symptoms - whole plant (stunting type, introduced in Korea)
features.description: Besides the 'bakanae symptom' that elongates stems, the Korean population includes a pathotype causing a 'stem blight symptom' that stunts stem growth and then kills the plant by drying. This pathotype cannot produce gibberellin during infection and produces fumonisins and fusaric acid. In Korea the proportion of the 'blight' pathotype is far higher than the 'bakanae' pathotype.
features.short_quote: "stunts stem growth and then kills the plant by drying" (translated from Korean)
features.source_name: Newsis 2017-11-07, "IPET identifies the stem-blight mechanism of rice bakanae for the first time in the world" (citing an announcement by the Korea Institute of Planning and Evaluation for Technology in Food, Agriculture and Forestry)
features.source_type: Other (news media; citing a public-agency announcement)

source_conflicts: Leaf color descriptions differ. NCPMS does not give the leaf color of elongated seedlings and uses 'light green' only for plants that die after maximum tillering without elongation. IRRI describes leaves of elongated plants as 'yellow-green or light green', and Niehaus 2017 describes stems and internodes as yellowish.

Position and timing of white mycelium and spores: NCPMS 'on sheaths 2–3 weeks after bakanae symptoms in the paddy field', IRRI 'white powder at the base or lower part', Kim C.K. 1981 'about 1 week after elongation, up to 40–60% of plant height'.

The status of the stunting type differs. NCPMS and IRRI treat it as an exception due to heavy seed infection or some infected plants, while Niehaus 2017 and the 2017 Newsis report state that the stunting type is the majority among Korean isolates (9 of 15 field isolates). The cause is also explained differently: NCPMS by degree of infection, the original paper by the isolate pathotype (no GA, fumonisin production).
Root symptoms appear only in IRRI (root lesions) and Niehaus (root colonization by the stunting type).
No source among those opened describes 'pink mycelium'; all mention only 'white'.
NCPMS gives *Gibberella fujikuroi* (Sawada) Ito, which differs from the international authority (Sawada) Wollenw.
diseases.photo_visible: Elongation of 1.5 times or more in the nursery, 1st–2nd leaf angle of 45° or more, thin pale leaves in the paddy field, white mycelium on sheaths and base, adventitious roots from upper nodes.
diseases.lab_required: Confirmation of stunting-type and symptomless infection (macroconidial morphology and PCR), determination of elongation vs stunting pathotype (molecular, GA/fumonisin analysis), latent seed infection.

diseases.intro: There are three Korean official sources (NCPMS, RDA press releases 2015 and 2024), a Korean original paper (In 1985), and an ultrastructure paper by Korean researchers (Kim & Park 2007). Chlamydospore size figures appear only in the overseas TNAU source.

features.description: Occurs only on grains. Initially the grain surface is yellow-green, so it is easy to recognize visually.
features.short_quote: "occurs only on grains; initially the grain surface is yellow-green" (translated from Korean)

features.description: Over time the hull opens slightly and a yellow-green protrusion is visible. Once powdery chlamydospores form on the surface it turns black.
features.short_quote: "turns black once powdery chlamydospores form" (translated from Korean)
features.location_in_source: Symptom description, second half of sentence 1

features.description: When the hull of an infected grain is removed, the inside is white and the outside dark green or black. It is easy to identify because it forms 'smut balls' (nuruk) on the panicle.
features.short_quote: "white inside but dark green or black outside" (translated from Korean)

features.description: Overwinters as sclerotia or chlamydospores. Sclerotia in the soil germinate around July–August the next year to form fruiting bodies; ascospores fly to leaf sheaths at booting and enter grains through the flowers around flowering. Low temperature with high humidity, lack of sunshine and number of rainy days have a decisive influence. There was a major outbreak in the central region in 1998.
features.short_quote: "environmental conditions such as low temperature and high humidity, lack of sunshine, number of rainy days" (translated from Korean)
features.plant_part: Leaf sheath to flower to grain

features.description: Early in the outbreak, round ball-shaped yellow-green protrusions (fungal spores) form on panicles and gradually turn black, so they are easy to confirm. It occurs readily when rain is frequent and humid around panicle emergence, temperatures are low at around 25 °C, and sunshine is scarce.
features.short_quote: "round, ball-shaped yellow-green protrusions (fungal spores)" (translated from Korean)
features.source_name: RDA press release 2024-08-01 "Stable rice production after the monsoon depends on disease management" (National Institute of Crop Science)

features.description: Occurs only on grains. Initially the grain surface is yellow-green, so it is easy to recognize visually. The pathogen enters through rice flowers at flowering.
features.short_quote: "initially the surface of rice grains is yellow-green" (translated from Korean)
features.source_name: RDA press release 2015-07-29 (reprinted on Korea Policy Briefing)

features.description: Velvety spore balls form on spikelets. Spore balls are orange at first and become greenish-black when mature. Individual grains are transformed into masses of spore balls.
features.short_quote: "initially orange and turn greenish black when mature"

features.description: Stage-by-stage photo captions: ① grain transformed into a velvety spore mass or yellow fruiting body ② spores grow and enclose the floral organs ③ immature spore balls are slightly flattened, smooth, yellow and enclosed by a membrane ④ spores grow and the membrane bursts ⑤ mature spores are orange, then become yellowish-green or greenish-black
features.short_quote: "Immature spores slightly flattened, smooth, yellow, and covered by a membrane"

features.description: Usually not all spikelets on a panicle are infected. Spikelets next to spore balls are often unfilled. Typically only a few grains per panicle are infected and the rest are normal.
features.short_quote: "spikelets neighboring smut balls are often unfilled"
features.location_in_source: How to identify, item 3 and last caption

features.description: Visible only after panicle emergence; infection can occur at flowering. Occurs at relative humidity >90% and 25–35 °C, favored by rain, high humidity and high-nitrogen soil. Damage appears in two phases: the ovary is destroyed early in flowering, and there is a second infection phase when spikelets are nearly mature.
features.short_quote: "visible only after panicle exsertion"
features.growth_stage: Infection at flowering; visible after heading
features.location_in_source: Why and where it occurs; Why is it important

features.description: Infected grains bear velvety green spore balls. Spore balls are small at first and gradually enlarge to a maximum of about 1 cm. They are visible between the glumes and enclose the floral organs.
features.short_quote: "grows gradually up to the size of 1 cm"
features.source_name: TNAU Agritech, Paddy expert system: False smut

features.description: As fungal growth intensifies, spore balls burst and turn orange, then yellowish-green or greenish-black. Infection usually occurs at the reproductive and grain-filling stages, and only a few grains per panicle are infected.
features.short_quote: "becomes orange then later yellowish-green or greenish-black"

features.description: Chlamydospores on spore balls are borne laterally on small sterigmata of radiating hyphae. They are globose to elliptical with warty surfaces, olive-colored, **3–5 × 4–6 µm**. Young spores are smaller, paler and almost smooth.
features.short_quote: "spherical to elliptical, warty, olivaceous, 3-5 x 4-6 µm"

features.description: Some green spore balls form 1–4 sclerotia in the center. Sclerotia overwinter in the field and produce stalked stromata in summer and autumn of the next year. Primary infection is thought to come mainly from sclerotium-derived ascospores, and secondary infection from chlamydospores.
features.short_quote: "develop one to four sclerotia in the center"

features.description: Under the light microscope, spores are round to elliptical with warty surfaces, about 3–5 µm in diameter. Under scanning electron microscopy, globose to irregularly round ornamented spores with distinct spines were seen. Spines are pointed or irregularly curved, about 200–500 nm long. The authors call these spores **conidia**.
features.short_quote: "diameters approximately ranging from 3 to 5 μm"
features.source_name: Kim K.W. & Park E.W. 2007, *Micron* 38(6):626–631 (abstract on Kyungpook National Univ. research portal)

features.description: Upland rice was more severely affected than paddy rice: more diseased grains per panicle, larger and heavier spore balls, and sclerotium formation on spore balls of 22.2% in upland rice versus 3.6% in paddy rice. Yellow chlamydospore balls germinated most vigorously, declining as they matured and darkened. Most diseased panicles had 1–5 infected grains, concentrated in the lower part of the panicle (near the first branch node).
features.short_quote: "yellow chlamydospores in the early formation stage germinate vigorously" (translated from Korean)
features.source_name: In M.S., Park J.S., Yu S.H. 1985, "Studies on the occurrence ecology of rice false smut" (in Korean), Research Reports of Agricultural Science (Chungnam National Univ.) 12(2):242–252

features.description: Overwintered sclerotia placed on the soil surface in early July germinated 81% within 19 days (May treatment: 60–70% in 41 days). They germinated at the surface to 1 cm depth at 25–30 °C, but not at 3 or 5 cm depth. Each sclerotium produced about 6 stromata, each with 50–140 perithecia. Injecting ascospores or chlamydospores into leaf sheaths at booting infected panicles. Spraying chlamydospores on seedlings was not pathogenic.

source_conflicts: The color sequence of spore balls differs between Korean and overseas sources. The three Korean official sources describe yellow-green to black; IRRI gives 'orange → greenish-black' in its text and 'immature, enclosed in yellow membrane → orange → yellowish-green or greenish-black' in photo captions; TNAU gives 'yellow fruiting body → orange on bursting → yellowish-green or greenish-black'. In 1985 describes early spore balls as 'yellow'. Korean official sources have no yellow or orange stage.
The final color is 'black' in NCPMS and RDA 2024, 'dark green or black' in the NCPMS cross-section, and 'greenish-black' in IRRI.

Spore terminology conflicts. TNAU calls them 'chlamydospores 3–5 × 4–6 µm', while Kim & Park 2007 call spores of the same form (round to elliptical, warty, about 3–5 µm) 'conidia'. Kim & Park 2007 is by Korean researchers but the sample origin is not given in the abstract.
Temperature for occurrence: RDA 2024 'when low at around 25 °C', NCPMS 'low temperature and high humidity', IRRI '25–35 °C, RH >90%'.
The spore ball size 'up to about 1 cm' appears only in TNAU. In 1985 adds Korean positional information that 1–5 grains cluster in the lower part of the panicle (near the first branch node).
diseases.photo_visible: Round velvety spore balls in place of grains, color stages from yellow, orange and yellow-green to greenish-black and black, only a few grains per panicle infected, white interior in cross-section.
diseases.lab_required: Chlamydospore shape, size and surface ornamentation (microscopy, SEM), sclerotial germination and ascospores (culture), official criteria for distinguishing from kernel smut (Unconfirmed).

diseases.intro: There are Korean official sources (NCPMS, two RDA press releases) and the first Korean report of *B. plantarii* (Ra 2016). Overseas descriptions (US FSA7580, Ham 2011, LSU) and the Japan-related *B. plantarii* seedling blight descriptions are not Korean data.

features.description: Occurs mainly on grains, but symptoms are also seen on leaf sheaths. Grains discolor yellowish-white starting from the base, gradually expanding until the whole grain is discolored.
features.short_quote: "grains discolor yellowish-white starting from the base" (translated from Korean)

features.description: In the field, panicles infected early turn pale red overall. They stand straight without bending down, and embryo development stops so the grains become empty.
features.short_quote: "panicles stand straight without bending down" (translated from Korean)

features.description: Brown rice from grains infected late is smaller than healthy rice and has brown streaks.
features.short_quote: "brown stripes develop" (translated from Korean)

features.description: When infected seed is sown, heavily infected seeds fail to germinate or rot. Seedlings from lightly infected seed have leaves that fail to unfold or sheaths that brown, grow poorly and eventually die.
features.short_quote: "leaf sheaths brown, growth is poor and plants eventually die" (translated from Korean)

features.description: Overwinters in seed and spreads to healthy seed during soaking. If the nursery is hot and humid it causes seedling rot around diseased seeds. Under unfavorable conditions it stays latent in sheaths of apparently healthy plants and enters grains when heading conditions are suitable.
