Major outbreaks occur when hot and humid at heading and flowering. Usually it develops readily at 10² CFU/mL of pathogen and air temperature of 20 °C or above.
features.short_quote: "major outbreaks when hot and humid at heading and flowering" (translated from Korean)
features.growth_stage: Seed soaking and seedling raising; heading and flowering

features.description: A short rod-shaped Gram-negative bacterium about 0.7 × 1.5–2.5 µm with 1–3 polar flagella. It forms a **light-green pigment** on King's medium B, distinguishing it from other bacteria. Its optimum growth temperature of 30–35 °C is higher than other plant pathogenic bacteria. Rice is its only natural host, and it causes seedling rot and grain rot. Seed transmission is possible.
features.short_quote: "forms a light-green pigment on King's medium B (KB)" (translated from Korean)

features.description: When infected, grains begin turning brown from where they are set just after heading, and the whole grain discolors. In severe cases panicles do not fill. It is frequent when high temperatures above 30 °C and high humidity continue around panicle emergence.
features.short_quote: "begins turning brown from where grains are set" (translated from Korean)
features.location_in_source: Body text, bacterial grain rot paragraph

features.description: More frequent the longer high temperatures above 30 °C continue around heading and flowering, or the more often rain of about 30 mm falls and humidity is high. It states that symptoms appear only on rice grains.
features.short_quote: "symptoms appear only on rice grains." (translated from Korean)
features.location_in_source: Body text, bacterial grain rot paragraph

features.description: Blighted grains on infected panicles initially have the lower third of the developing grain white to light gray, separated by a dark-brown boundary (Fig. 1).
features.short_quote: "white to light gray with a dark-brown margin on the bottom third"
features.source_name: Univ. of Arkansas Div. of Agriculture, FSA7580 "Bacterial Panicle Blight of Rice in Arkansas"(Wamishe et al.)

features.description: Early in infection the rachis and panicle branches stay green (Fig. 2). Grains then turn straw-colored, and by the end of the season can darken further due to secondary fungi (Fig. 3).
features.short_quote: "rachis or panicle branches stay green during early infection"
features.growth_stage: Early stage to end of season

features.description: Severely infected panicles stay upright because the grains do not fill (blanking) (Fig. 4). Severely infected grains have a black rotted base and the seed degenerates (Fig. 5).
features.short_quote: "aborted seeds with a dark basal rot"

features.description: On some tillers dark-brown lesions form on the flag leaf sheath (Fig. 6), and such tillers may have severe panicle damage (Fig. 7).
features.short_quote: "dark brown lesion on the flag leaf sheath"

features.description: Can be confused with wind damage (Fig. 8), water stress (Fig. 9), other environmental factors and insect damage such as stem borers.

Mainly seed-borne, but the main symptoms appear at heading. Favored by prolonged high night temperatures in summer, and long dew periods also increase disease. It can also cause seedling death, but this stage is not well known in the USA.
features.short_quote: "favored by extended periods of hot summer nights"

features.description: Linear lesions extend downward from the collar on the flag leaf sheath. They can be several inches long with reddish-brown borders and gray necrotic centers.
features.short_quote: "reddish-brown border and a grey, necrotic centre"
features.source_name: Ham J.H., Melanson R.A., Rush M.C. 2011, "*Burkholderia glumae*: next major pathogen of rice?", *Mol. Plant Pathol.* 12(4):329–339
features.location_in_source: Symptoms of bacterial panicle blight; Fig. 1A–B

features.description: One or all florets dry, and grains fail to fill or degenerate. The basal third of the floret is initially white to light gray, separated from the rest by a reddish-brown boundary, and later turns straw-colored. In severely affected fields, upright brown panicles with unfilled grains are typical.
features.short_quote: "Upright brown panicles"
features.location_in_source: Symptoms of bacterial panicle blight; Fig. 1

features.description: Depending on growth stage it causes grain rot, sheath rot and seedling rot. Visible symptoms appear first on the flag leaf sheath and then on the panicle. Flag-leaf-sheath symptoms predict later panicle disease. Heading and flowering are the most vulnerable stages. Unusually high temperatures (especially at night) and frequent rain at heading and flowering cause epidemics.
Gram-negative, aerobic, motile, pectolytic rods, 0.5–0.7 × 1.5–2.5 µm, with 2–4 polar flagella. Grows at 11–40 °C with an optimum of 30–35 °C; GC content about 68.2%.
features.short_quote: "0.5–0.7 × 1.5–2.5 µm" (figures as in original)

features.description: On King's B agar, toxoflavin appears as a **yellow pigment** around colonies (Fig. 1D). On CPG agar it produces visible amounts of extracellular polysaccharide (EPS). On LB + 0.2% Tween-20, lipase activity appears as an opaque iridescent halo (Fig. 1E). On pectate semi-solid medium, pectinase pitting occurs (Fig. 1F). The semi-selective medium S-PG is used for isolation and identification.
features.short_quote: "yellow pigment" (King's B, Fig. 1D description)

features.category: Culture characteristics / pathogen morphology (role of toxoflavin)
features.description: Toxoflavin, fervenulin and reumycin are phytotoxins, and toxoflavin is the most toxic to rice. It reduces stem and root elongation of seedlings and causes the characteristic grain rot on panicles. However, toxoflavin-deficient mutants still cause weak panicle symptoms.

*B. glumae* and *B. plantarii* were moved together from *Pseudomonas* to *Burkholderia* in 1994 and are phylogenetically close. 16S–23S rDNA spacer primers can distinguish them, and gyrB multiplex PCR distinguishes *B. glumae*, *B. gladioli* and *B. plantarii*. *B. gladioli* also causes grain rot, seedling rot and panicle blight but is isolated less often and is less virulent (estimated at about 20% of panicle blight in Louisiana and elsewhere, unpublished).

Shows the characteristic "two-tone" discoloration of grains, upright discolored panicles with green stems, and patches of upright discolored panicles in the field. Very early infection appears as water-soaked discoloration of the lower grain, and late infection as secondary fungal growth. The same pathogen also causes sheath rot.
features.short_quote: "characteristic two tone discoloration symptom"
features.source_name: LSU AgCenter, Rice Diseases Photo Galleries: Bacterial Panicle Blight
features.location_in_source: List of photo captions ("Characteristic Two Tone…", "Discolored Heads and Green Stems", "Early… Pathogen Infection", "Bacterial Panicle Blight Pathogen 2·3")

features.category: Symptoms - panicle/grain / Symptoms - sheath/stem (*B. plantarii*, Korea)
features.description: In September 2015, bacterial grain rot panicles showing grain degeneration and hull and grain discoloration were collected from a paddy in Suncheon. Of 66 isolates obtained on King's B medium, PCR screening yielded 2 isolates (including GRBB 15061 = KACC 18964), confirmed as *B. plantarii* by 16S rRNA, rpoD and gyrB sequences. Stem injection at tillering reproduced sheath rot, and panicle spraying at heading reproduced grain rot. The authors state this is the first report in Korea.
features.short_quote: "grain abortion, discoloration of the hull and grain"
features.source_name: Ra J.E. et al. 2016, "First report of bacterial grain rot caused by *Burkholderia plantarii* in Republic of Korea", *J. Plant Pathol.* 98(3)

features.description: Seedlings died in about half of the nursery boxes. Symptoms are basal yellowing and wilting of the 2nd and 3rd leaves; over time infected seedlings dry up reddish-brown and die.
features.short_quote: "basal chlorosis and withering of second and third leaves"
features.source_name: World Encyclopedia of Plant Bacterial Diseases (PlantDiseases.org), "Bacterial seedling blight / Rice" photo entry (SOURCE: K. Azegami, M. Goto)

features.description: Basal yellowing and wilting of the 2nd and 3rd leaves appear, and seedlings dry reddish-brown over time. Root growth is delayed so seedlings fall over easily. Another photo entry (SOURCE: H. Honma, M. Goto) describes brown, dried nursery seedlings as the same symptom.
features.short_quote: "Root growth is retarded and seedlings easily lodge."
features.source_name: PlantDiseases.org, "Bacterial seedling blight / Rice"(SOURCE: K. Azegami)

source_conflicts: Early grain color: NCPMS 'yellowish-white from the base', RDA 2024 'brown from where grains are set', FSA7580 'lower third white to light gray + dark-brown boundary', Ham 2011 'reddish-brown boundary', LSU 'two-tone'. All agree it starts at the base.
Panicle color: NCPMS 'pale red', Ham 'upright brown panicles', FSA 'straw-colored, then darkened by secondary fungi'.
There is a conflict on sheath symptoms. NCPMS, Ham, FSA, LSU and Ra 2016 describe sheath symptoms, but the RDA 2015 press release says 'symptoms appear only on rice grains'.
Cell size and flagella number differ: NCPMS 0.7 × 1.5–2.5 µm with 1–3 polar flagella, Ham 2011 0.5–0.7 × 1.5–2.5 µm with 2–4 polar flagella.
The pigment on King's B medium is 'light green' in NCPMS and the 'yellow pigment' of toxoflavin in Ham 2011. NCPMS does not explicitly identify this pigment as toxoflavin.
Temperature: NCPMS 'develops readily at 20 °C or above' (reads as a minimum condition), press releases 'sustained above 30 °C' (reads as an outbreak condition).

The pathogen scope differs. NCPMS lists only *B. glumae*, Ra 2016 reports Korean occurrence caused by *B. plantarii*, and Ham and LSU also cite *B. gladioli* as a cause. The main symptom of *B. plantarii* is seedling blight in Japan-related sources, and grain rot plus sheath rot in Ra 2016.
diseases.photo_visible: Two-tone discoloration starting from the grain base (lower third), upright panicles with unfilled grains and a rachis that stays green, brown linear lesions on the flag leaf sheath.
diseases.lab_required: Distinguishing the causal species (*glumae*/*plantarii*/*gladioli*) (16S–23S spacer and gyrB PCR), toxoflavin pigment on KB medium and isolation on S-PG (culture), definitive separation from wind, water stress and insect damage.

diseases.scientific_name: Rice stripe virus, vector Laodelphax striatellus
diseases.intro: There are Korean official sources (Nongsaro rice stripe and small brown planthopper pages) and three Korean original papers (Chung 1974, Lee 2004, Lee 2012). The NCPMS detail page did not open this time.

features.description: As an early symptom, small yellow-green spots form at the leaf base, and all leaves emerging afterwards show symptoms
features.short_quote: "small yellow-green spots at the leaf base" (translated from Korean)
features.source_name: Nongsaro pest information "Rice stripe (縞葉枯病, Stripe)"

features.description: Young seedlings infected late in the nursery show new leaves turning yellow, rolling, drooping and dying early after transplanting
features.short_quote: "new leaves turn yellow, roll, droop and die" (translated from Korean)
features.growth_stage: Infection late in nursery bed, then early after transplanting

features.description: With late infection, yellowish-white lesions form on the flag leaf. Severe cases may be stunted, but plants usually look like healthy plants
features.short_quote: "yellowish-white lesions on the flag leaf" (translated from Korean)

features.description: The typical symptom is broad yellow stripes or chlorosis. Leaves fail to unfold normally, elongate and twist or droop downward
features.short_quote: "elongate and twist or droop downward" (translated from Korean)

features.description: Diseased plants have fewer tillers and fail to head. Even if they head, panicles are malformed or absent, and even when panicles form, incomplete emergence is common
features.short_quote: "even if panicles emerge, they are malformed" (translated from Korean)

features.description: Resistant cultivars rarely die, and large and small yellow-green lesions appear irregularly
Symptoms begin to appear late in the nursery or around June, and are most frequent from about July 20 to early August
features.growth_stage: Late nursery bed to early August

features.description: Infection occurs up to the 7-leaf stage late in the nursery, and about 50% die if infected up to the 9-leaf stage

Susceptible japonica plants infected at the 3rd–7th leaf stage die 100%. Mortality is about 50% at the 9-leaf stage and about 20% at the 11-leaf stage, with no dead plants after the 13-leaf stage. The latent period is 7–15 days for inoculation at the 3rd–7th leaf stage and 15–30 days at the 9th–15th leaf stage
features.short_quote: "plants died 100% when infected" (translated from Korean)
features.source_name: Chung 1974, Korean Journal of Applied Entomology 13(4):181–204
features.location_in_source: Abstract 1 (occurrence, damage by leaf stage, latent period)

features.description: Diseased plants are more numerous in rows near the levee and decrease toward the center. Disease is heavier in early-season cultivation
Infected rice stems wilt, yellow and die, or if they survive they set almost no grain. Infection after the 11th true-leaf stage causes little yield loss
features.source_name: Nongsaro insect pest information "Small brown planthopper (striatellus)"

features.description: Chlorotic to yellowish-white stripes, mottling and necrotic streaks form on leaves
features.short_quote: "chlorotic to yellowish white stripes, mottling, and necrotic streaks"
features.source_name: Lucid/IRRI-ACIAR-UQ Rice Doctor fact sheet "Stripe (Rice stripe virus)"

features.description: Infected seedlings have leaves that fold, twist, wilt and droop. Plants are stunted with few tillers and panicles and may die early

Panicles are white to brown with malformed, sterile florets and may not emerge fully. With infection after maximum tillering, chlorosis and mottling are mild and heading and grain filling may be delayed
The seedling to early tillering stage is most susceptible. The danger period is when viruliferous insects migrate in large numbers from overwintering winter cereals
features.location_in_source: Why and where it occurs / How to manage

features.description: Chlorotic stripes and yellowing, moderate stunting and reduced vigor. In severe cases brown to gray necrotic streaks form on leaves and plants die. Panicles are few or absent, and those that form are malformed and discolored (citing Toriyama 2000)
Slightly stunted but tiller number is normal. Pale green stripes or mottling and necrotic streaks on leaves
features.short_quote: "Faded green stripe or mottling and necrotic streaks"

features.description: *Tenuivirus* particles are thin filaments 2–2.5 nm in diameter, sometimes appearing helical, branched or panhandle-shaped. Length 200–3,000 nm (proportional to genome segment size). No envelope. 4–6 segments of negative-sense and ambisense single-stranded RNA
features.short_quote: "Thin, filamentous"
features.location_in_source: Chapter body text (virion morphology and genome description)

features.description: A non-structural protein (NCP) forms inclusion bodies in infected cells and is presumed to be related to symptom expression
RT-PCR is used to diagnose diseased plants in Korea (photos of diseased plants from Seocheon and Miryang, Fig. 1; RT-PCR detection, Fig. 2). The paper contains almost no symptom description
features.source_name: Lee et al. 2012, Research in Plant Disease 18(4):402–405
features.location_in_source: Fig. 1 and Fig. 2 captions, body text

features.description: States explicitly that RSV symptoms are very hard to distinguish visually from physiological disorders, and develops a precise RT-PCR diagnosis
features.source_name: Lee et al. 2004, Research in Plant Disease 10(1):30–33

features.description: Adult small brown planthoppers have the sides of the back darker than the middle (the brown planthopper does not). Brown planthoppers live in groups while small brown planthoppers are scattered. Planthoppers in barley fields in April–May can be regarded as small brown planthoppers. Eggs are laid in leaf sheaths in groups of 3–10, about 400 on average
features.short_quote: "both sides of the back darker than the middle" (translated from Korean)
features.plant_part: Lower part of rice hill, leaf sheath

features.description: Adults have macropterous (long-winged) and brachypterous (short-winged) forms. Wings are transparent and the body, mesonotum and frontal area are black to dark brown. The deep black area between the carinae of the frons is the most reliable diagnostic character. The abdomen is milky white to black. Nymphs have 5 instars, and the 5th-instar head width is 0.50–0.54 mm. Eggs are white and laid in masses of 60–260
features.short_quote: "deep black color ... frons ... is diagnostic"

features.description: Transmitted in a persistent, circulative-propagative manner, mainly by the small brown planthopper. *Unkanodes sapporona*, *U. albifascia* and *Terthron albovittatum* also transmit it
There is transovarial transmission and transmission via sperm

Second-generation adult small brown planthoppers settle on young rice in the paddy field in May–June and transmit in earnest. They migrate en masse from China to the southwest coast in late May to early June
features.source_name: Nongsaro "Rice stripe" disease environment; Nongsaro "Small brown planthopper" ecology information
features.location_in_source: Disease environment sentence 4; ecology information sentence 6

source_conflicts: Severity with late infection: Nongsaro says 'plants usually look like healthy plants', while Lucid says 'chlorosis and mottling are mild, with delayed heading and grain filling', so the range differs.
Degree of stunting: Nongsaro 'stunted in severe cases', Lucid 'stunted' (seedling infection), Wang 2022 'slightly dwarf', CAPS (citing Toriyama 2000) 'moderate stunting'.
Tillering conflicts: Wang 2022 says 'normal', Nongsaro and Lucid say 'reduced' (that this may reflect infection timing is an inference in the notes).
Stripe color: Nongsaro 'broad yellow' (yellow-green in resistant cultivars, yellowish-white with late infection), Lucid 'chlorotic to yellowish-white', Wang 'faded green'.
Mortality figures by leaf stage are more specific in Chung 1974 (100% at 3rd–7th leaf, about 50% at 9th, about 20% at 11th) than in Nongsaro; both sources agree on 50% at the 9th leaf stage.

Sap transmission: the ICTV *Tenuivirus* chapter states that mechanical transmission by sap is possible, but Nongsaro says there is no seed, contact or soil transmission. The experimental conditions behind the ICTV statement are Unconfirmed.
Nongsaro D00004257 'rice stripe' is a page for proso millet and must not be confused with the rice page (D00000740).
diseases.photo_visible: Yellow-green spots at the base of new leaves, broad yellow stripes, new leaves rolling and drooping (death of young seedlings), poor heading and malformed panicles, concentration in rows near the levee.
diseases.lab_required: RT-PCR confirmation (Korean researchers state visual separation from physiological disorders is very difficult), particles and inclusion bodies (electron microscopy), identification of the small brown planthopper (frontal carinae, stereo microscope).

diseases.scientific_name: Rice dwarf virus, vectors Nephotettix cincticeps and others
diseases.intro: There are Korean official sources (Nongsaro rice dwarf and green rice leafhopper pages), and an international organization (ICTV) and a Nepal original paper (JIRCAS) give particle morphology. Korean occurrence is currently described as local occurrence in parts of the south.

features.description: The whole leaf turns dark green, yellowish or white spots form on the leaf surface, and the plant is severely stunted
features.short_quote: "the whole leaf turns dark green" (translated from Korean)
features.source_name: Nongsaro pest information "Rice dwarf (萎縮病, Dwarf)"

features.description: Spots vary in size and together form stripes confined along the veins
features.short_quote: "stripes confined along the veins" (translated from Korean)

features.description: Spots are also seen on the leaf sheath
In some cases the tips of old leaves turn yellow, and the yellowing spreads along the leaf margins
features.plant_part: Tips and margins of old leaves

features.description: Tillering is usually abnormally excessive, but infection early in growth actually reduces tiller number. Root growth is severely stunted and fine roots tend to spread horizontally
features.short_quote: "fine roots tend to spread horizontally" (translated from Korean)

features.description: Diseased rice survives to harvest in a dark green or pale green state, but fails to form panicles or has few, poorly filled grains. Dark-brown blotches form on grains, and dark-brown spots may also appear on brown rice
features.short_quote: "dark-brown spots also on brown rice" (translated from Korean)

features.description: Mostly develops around late July at the end of tillering, and in early-season cultivation may develop at heading. In Korea it has occurred since 1965, with a major outbreak in 1973, expanding from the south to Chungnam, Chungbuk and Gangwon

Viruliferous green rice leafhoppers overwinter on levees, banks and in cracks in the paddy floor, and first-generation adults fly to the nursery and infect seedlings. First-generation nymphs, second-generation adults and nymphs, and third-generation adults cause the most damage. Transmitted transovarially
Rice dwarf currently occurs only locally in parts of the southern region, and the area affected is small
features.short_quote: "only locally in parts of the southern region" (translated from Korean)
features.source_name: Nongsaro insect pest information "Green rice leafhopper (cincticeps)"

features.description: White flecks and streaks form on leaves, plants are stunted and produce excessive tillers. Stunted plants fail to set seed. No galls, enations or tumors are formed
features.short_quote: "white flecks and streaks on leaves"

features.description: Stunted with increased tillering. Leaves are short and dark green with fine chlorotic specks
features.short_quote: "dark green in color with fine chlorotic specks"

features.description: The characteristic symptoms are stunting and white chlorotic specks on the leaves (citing Iida et al. 1972). In Nepal, plants showing white chlorotic specks at tillering were sampled. Less than 1% of hills were diseased, and infection appeared to have occurred at early tillering
features.short_quote: "white chlorotic specks on foliage"
features.source_name: Omura et al., "Rice dwarf virus", JIRCAS TECHTARC No.21 pp.78–83
features.source_type: Original paper (published by international research institute)

features.description: Polyhedral particles about 70 nm with an electron-dense core in the center. They are scattered in the cytoplasm of chlorotic tissue cells and absent from nuclei, mitochondria and chloroplasts. Confirmed by serological methods such as agar gel diffusion and latex agglutination
features.short_quote: "Polyhedral particles about 70 nm in diameter"

features.description: Icosahedral particles with a distinctly angular appearance. RDV is about 70 nm in diameter with a double-shelled structure (outer: 260 P8 trimers, T=13; inner: 60 P3 dimers). The genome is 12 segments of linear dsRNA
features.short_quote: "distinctive angular appearance"
features.location_in_source: Chapter body text (virion morphology and genome description)

features.description: Among plant reoviruses, RDV is the only one not restricted to the phloem

The green rice leafhopper is a green leafhopper visible to the naked eye. Together with the white-backed planthopper and small brown planthopper it is one of the most common pests of rice. Eggs are long-oval, about 1 mm long, laid in a row of 3–20 in leaf sheaths. It overwinters as 3rd–4th (or 4th) instar nymphs in weeds on south-facing levees
features.short_quote: "green leafhoppers can be observed with the naked eye" (translated from Korean)

features.description: Transmitted propagatively by leafhoppers (Cicadellidae). *N. cincticeps* is most important, and *N. nigropictus*, *Recilia dorsalis* and some *Nephotettix* spp. also transmit. The latent period in the insect is about 10–20 days, after which it transmits for life. Transovarial transmission via the route of the symbiont *Candidatus* Sulcia muelleri. No sap or seed transmission
Persistent-propagative with transovarial transmission. Circulative period 12–25 days. Vectors are *N. cincticeps* (main), *R. dorsalis*, *N. virescens* and *N. nigropictus*
The only known vector in Nepal is *N. nigropictus*. In Kathmandu it occurs from April to November, peaking in August–September

source_conflicts: Spot color: Nongsaro 'yellowish or white', ICTV 'white flecks and streaks', JIRCAS 'white chlorotic specks', Wang 'fine chlorotic specks'.
The directional pattern 'along the veins' is stated only by Nongsaro.
On tillering, ICTV and Wang mention only excess or increase, while Nongsaro adds the exception of reduced tillering and root stunting (horizontal spread of fine roots) with early infection.
For panicles and grains, ICTV says 'fails to set seed' while Nongsaro goes as far as 'dark-brown spots on grains and brown rice'. Grain spots could not be confirmed in international sources.
The period within the insect differs in definition and figures: ICTV latent period about 10–20 days, Wang 2022 circulative period 12–25 days.

For Korean status, the Nongsaro rice dwarf page describes the 1973 outbreak and regional expansion, while the green rice leafhopper page describes current local occurrence in parts of the south, so they refer to different times.

Comparison clue: the notes state that if galls are present, black-streaked dwarf should be considered instead (Nongsaro D00000738: white enations on leaf-underside veins and stems at heading turning brown to black).
diseases.photo_visible: Dark green leaves with white spots aligned along the veins, severe stunting and excessive tillering, no galls on the leaf underside, green rice leafhoppers.
diseases.lab_required: Polyhedral particles about 70 nm (electron microscopy), serological and molecular tests, confirmation of vector species.

diseases.intro: No Korean source confirmed. No Korean record of udbatta on rice, nor an official list entry for the Korean name 'byeo-isak-mira-byeong', was found; everything below is from Indian and Japanese sources (the Japanese JARQ paper concerns forage-grass isolates).

features.description: A white mycelial mat binds the panicle branches so the panicle emerges as an upright, dirty-colored cylindrical rod. No grains form on diseased panicles
features.short_quote: "much resembling an agarbatti or udbattta"
features.source_name: TNAU Agritech Portal, Expert System for Paddy "Udbatta disease"

features.description: Before heading, white mycelium and conidia form narrow streaks along the veins of the flag leaf
Grayish-white mycelium grows on young leaves of infected seedlings, suggesting that infection occurs during germination

Externally seed-borne and systemic. Since diseased panicles do not set grain, infected seed is of low importance as inoculum. Alternative hosts are *Isachne elegans*, *Cynodon dactylon*, *Pennisetum* sp. and *Eragrostis tenuifolia*
Favored by high temperature and humidity and by the maximum tillering to panicle initiation stage. Disease is low with very early or very late sowing

A minor disease present only in some areas (mainly highlands). It has no noticeable effect on growth or appearance, so diseased plants cannot be identified until heading. Heading is similar to or slightly earlier than healthy plants

Instead of a normal panicle, a rod-like structure ("agarbathi") emerges from the flag leaf. Masses of mycelium and spores bind the florets to the axis, forming a hard crust. Usually all tillers of a hill are infected, showing that infection is systemic
features.short_quote: "rod-shaped structure"

features.description: Not distinguishable until the flag leaf stage. Diseased panicles emerge as upright, grayish-white cylindrical structures resembling an incense stick (agarbatti), replacing the normal panicle. Diseased plants have all panicles infected, and even one infected panicle means complete yield loss for that panicle
features.short_quote: "erect, grayish-white, cylindrical structures"
features.source_name: Vineeth et al. 2025, Mysore J. Agric. Sci. 59(3):428–444

features.description: Common in low hill areas of Bihar, Odisha, Maharashtra and Karnataka, India, where soil temperatures are high (about 28 °C) and humid. In 2018, disease incidence reached up to 50% in cultivar Tunga in Karnataka and 10–30% in BR2655 and MTU 1001. In 2022–24 it was severe in major cultivars such as Jyothi and Jaya

The pathogen was isolated from diseased panicles by the spore drop method. On PDA, colonies are raised and cottony with a leathery, waxy texture. Identified by colony characteristics and conidia (named *E. japonica*)
features.short_quote: "elevated, fluffy, with a leathery and waxy texture"
features.location_in_source: Results and Discussion – Isolation of the Pathogen

features.description: (Forage grasses, not rice) The fungus covers the inflorescence and prevents it from unfolding, giving a mummified appearance. Mature stromata are grayish-white to black depending on maturity and host, and grayish-black sclerotium-like structures 1–2 mm in diameter may form on the panicle
features.short_quote: "Sclerotia-like structures, grayish black and 1–2 mm"

features.description: (Japanese grass isolates) Conidiophores arise in a palisade on the stroma, and conidia form from slender phialides at the tips. Conidia are colorless, needle-shaped, aseptate, 8.8–27.9 × 0.9–2.7 µm, with one nucleus (DAPI staining). The abstract gives 10–25 × 0.5–1 µm. The sexual stage was not observed in nature
features.short_quote: "colorless, needle-shaped, non-septate"

features.description: (Grasses) Mycelium grows epiphytically on the leaf surface forming white leaf streaks. SEM shows hyphal strands bearing masses of conidia extending epiphytically on the leaf surface, with no tissue penetration observed
There are no reports on rice in Japan. Since there is no difference in the original descriptions of *E. oryzae* and *E. japonica*, *E. japonica* is adopted by priority
Preferred name *Balansia oryzae-sativae* Hashioka. Synonyms *Balansia oryzae*, *Ephelis oryzae* Sydow. English names black choke, false ergot, incense rod, udbatta

Mature stromata form on the inflorescence and contain perithecia. Immature stromata have cup- to cushion-shaped black conidiomata. Conidia are colorless, filiform to needle-shaped, about 18–22 × 1.5 µm. With age the inflorescence darkens and pseudosclerotia form, giving a mummified look **(search snippet; original returned 403 and is Unconfirmed; host and region also Unconfirmed)**
Describes the sexual stage as *Balansia oryzae-sativae*, with the micrograph caption reading "*Ephelis oryzae*". No description of stroma, sclerotium or conidial sizes

source_conflicts: Panicle color: TNAU 'dirty-colored', Vineeth 2025 'grayish-white', JARQ (grasses) 'grayish-white to black', APS snippet 'darkens with age'.
Disease environment contrasts KAU 'a minor disease in some highland areas' with Vineeth 2025 'low hill areas, high temperature (about 28 °C), humid, recently severe in Karnataka'.
On leaf symptoms, TNAU describes white streaks along flag-leaf veins, but KAU says there is no change in appearance before heading.

Conidial size differs within the same JARQ paper (text 8.8–27.9 × 0.9–2.7 µm, abstract 10–25 × 0.5–1 µm), and the APS snippet (original 403) gives 18–22 × 1.5 µm. The JARQ figures are not from rice isolates.
Scientific names: TNAU and EPPO use *B. oryzae-sativae*/*E. oryzae*; Vineeth 2025 and JARQ use *E. japonica*.
A 'twisted neck' was not confirmed in udbatta sources (that feature belongs to ufra).
diseases.photo_visible: At heading the whole panicle emerges as an upright cylindrical rod (incense-stick shape) with no grains, all tillers of a hill infected, white streaks along flag-leaf veins before heading.
diseases.lab_required: Needle-shaped aseptate conidia (microscopy), colony characteristics (culture), molecular identification such as ITS (possibly unrecorded in Korea).

diseases.intro: No Korean source confirmed. There is no Korean occurrence record, and it is recorded as a quarantine pest per EPPO (per the notes). Everything below comes from deepwater rice areas of South and Southeast Asia and US agency material.

features.description: From seedling to flag leaf stage the main symptom is leaf chlorosis. Plants become deformed, and distinct white patches or splash-pattern spots form at the base of young leaves
features.short_quote: "speckles in a splash pattern"

features.description: Necrotic brown stains form on leaves and sheaths and gradually darken, and parts of the upper internodes turn dark brown. Leaf sheaths become deformed
The bases of young leaves twist, and **lower nodes may swell and branch irregularly**
features.short_quote: "lower nodes can become swollen with irregular branching"

features.description: Depending on severity, chlorotic parts, tillers or whole hills wilt and die, appearing light brown. In severe cases the whole crop is affected and dark-brown patches form in the field (usually after panicle initiation)

After heading, panicles are usually crinkled, and glumes, especially at the base, are empty and shriveled. Panicles and flag leaves twist and distort. Panicles are completely enclosed in a swollen sheath, emerge only partly, or are sterile
features.short_quote: "enclosed within a swollen sheath"

features.description: At harvest, stems carrying healthy panicles lodge, while infected stems carrying empty panicles stand upright (citing Cox & Rahman 1980)
features.short_quote: "remain erect"

features.description: Early on, nematodes hide inside the leaf sheath and are hard to detect. At the vegetative stage there is chlorosis, deformation, white splash spots at the base of young leaves, brown necrosis on leaves and sheaths, twisting of leaf bases, sheath deformation, swollen lower nodes and irregular branching. Later, dark-brown patches, partial heading, panicles inside swollen sheaths, sterility, empty panicles and upright stems at harvest appear

Early symptoms are hard to recognize. At about 2 months, white patches or splash patterns of dots and dashes at the leaf base, mosaic-like discoloration, chlorosis, and white streaks on young leaves and sheaths appear. The most typical and distinct symptoms are seen at heading. By severity and timing it is divided into **thor ufra (swollen ufra)** and **pucca ufra (ripe ufra)**, and there is also a three-grade system of ufra-I, II and III
features.short_quote: "thor ufra" / "pucca ufra"
features.growth_stage: About 2 months after transplanting to heading
features.source_name: Das D. 2024, "Ufra – The Deeply Mysterious Disease", Indian J. Nematology 53(Spl):49–60

features.description: In swollen ufra the panicle remains enclosed in the sheath; in ripe ufra the panicle emerges but grains set only partly at the tip **(search snippet; original Unconfirmed due to DNS error)**

Emerging and already emerged leaves show mosaic or chlorotic discoloration, yellowish or pale green splash patterns on leaves and sheaths, brown to dark-brown spots on leaves, and corrugated leaf margins. With early infection panicles fail to emerge
features.short_quote: "mosaic or chlorotic discolouration"

features.description: In irrigated and deepwater rice in Bangladesh, symptoms usually appear in late July to August. Symptoms appear within 1 week in young plants and within 10–15 days in plants around flowering

First observed about 2 months after transplanting. Early heading is the best time for surveys, and the most distinct symptoms appear on panicles (Ou 1985). Low-density infections are hard to find visually

15 females (Joydevpur, Bangladesh): L=0.8–1.20 mm, a=50–62, b=6–9, c=18–24, V=78–80, stylet 10–11 µm. 10 males: L=0.7–1.18 mm, spicules 16–21 µm, stylet 10 µm. Juveniles L=0.5–0.7 mm, stylet 8–10 µm. Butler (1913) original description of females: L=0.7–1.1 (0.9) mm, width 15–22 µm, V=70–80, stylet 9–10 µm, eggs 80–88 × 16–20 µm
features.short_quote: "spear =10-11 µm"

features.description: The female body is slender, nearly straight or slightly curved ventrally when relaxed. The lip region is unannulated, low and flat. The lateral field is 1/4 or less of body width with 4 lateral lines. The stylet is moderately developed, with the conus about 45% of stylet length and small distinct knobs (about 2 µm). The posterior oesophageal bulb is clavate (27–34 µm) and slightly overlaps the intestine. The ovary extends forward with oocytes in 1 row (rarely 2). The post-uterine sac is 2.0–2.5 times the body width at the vulva. **The tail is conoid, 5.2–5.4 times the anal body width, with a sharp tip that looks like a mucro.** Males are as numerous as females and the bursa extends nearly to the tail tip
features.short_quote: "tapering to a sharply pointed terminus resembling a mucro"

features.description: Distinguished from other species by tail shape and size, the relative lengths of stylet and post-uterine sac, and the number of lateral lines (Fortuner 1982). Females are slender, 0.8–1.2 mm long, with a slender pointed tail. The head is pale, the stylet small but distinct, and the vulva posterior

*Aphelenchoides besseyi* (white tip nematode) has oesophageal glands extensively overlapping the anterior intestine, 3–4 processes at the tail tip, males without a bursa, and oocytes in 2–4 rows in the female ovary. In contrast, *D. angustus* males have a bursa and female oocytes are mainly in 1 row
features.location_in_source: p.10 Easily Confused Pests; p.3 Pest Description

features.description: About 1.25 mm long, thread-like and slender, tapering at both ends. Swims actively; when dry it coils and becomes inactive, and resumes activity on contact with water or rain

Cutting rolled leaves and stems into about 55 mm pieces and soaking them in water, or dissecting young inflorescences, yields many active nematodes from fresh tissue. They are not found in internodes below the growing point. In dry panicles they take time to resume activity

An obligate ectoparasitic nematode feeding on young leaf tissue, found on leaves, inflorescences, young seeds and rolled stems. At harvest it lies dormant inside the dry glumes of lower florets and is not inside the grain

Found in the apical bud a few days after transplanting and feeds on newly formed bud tissue. The same page gives conflicting descriptions of ectoparasitism (Feeding) and migratory endoparasitism (Economic Importance)
Deformation, stunting and wilting of host tissue, sheath deformation, flower sterility, lesions on upper nodes. Yield can fall by 50% or more

source_conflicts: Nematode length: CAPS measurement table females 0.7–1.23 mm (compiled from several descriptions), CAPS identification section 0.8–1.2 mm, Banglapedia about 1.25 mm.
V value: Timm specimens 78–80, Butler original description 70–80.

The tail is conoid with a sharp mucro-like tip in the CAPS description, while the Assam specimens cited by CAPS (Das & Bajaj 2008) differ from earlier descriptions, for example with a short conoid tail.
Node symptoms are described differently: CAPS and CDFA 'swollen lower nodes', Nemaplex 'lesions on upper nodes'.
Ufra types (thor/swollen, pucca/ripe) appear only in the Das 2024 abstract and NRRI (snippet only).
Mode of parasitism: CAPS says 'obligate ectoparasite', while Nemaplex mixes ectoparasitism and migratory endoparasitism on the same page.
Leaf spot color: CAPS 'white splash', Banglapedia 'yellowish or pale green splash', Das 'white patches, dots and dashes, mosaic'.
diseases.photo_visible: White splash spots at the base of young leaves, twisting of leaf bases, dark browning of upper internodes, panicles inside swollen sheaths or with grain only at the tip, empty panicles standing upright at harvest.
diseases.lab_required: After extracting nematodes by soaking, confirm the tail, 4 lateral lines and male bursa (microscopy); differentiate from *Aphelenchoides besseyi*, which occurs in Korea.
